blueprintTopic: Gestational diabetes initial nutrition therapy
vignette: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, comes in at 26 weeks for a scheduled 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. She has no history of diabetes. Body mass index is 31 kg/m2. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Fasting plasma glucose is 96 mg/dL, the 1-hour value is 192 mg/dL, and the 2-hour value is 140 mg/dL. She feels well and the fetal heart rate is 148/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Medical nutrition therapy and home glucose monitoring
A confirmatory 100-g glucose tolerance test
Glyburide each morning as the initial drug
Hospital admission for an intravenous insulin infusion
Postpartum testing with no prenatal therapy
correctAnswer: Medical nutrition therapy and home glucose monitoring
explanation: One abnormal value on a 75-g one-step test (fasting at least 92 mg/dL or 1-hour at least 180 mg/dL) establishes gestational diabetes. Initial care is medical nutrition therapy, activity, and glucose monitoring. Pharmacotherapy is added only when monitoring stays above target. "Hospital admission for an intravenous insulin infusion" is not the best choice because A single diagnostic glucose in this range is not ketoacidosis or hyperglycemia that requires an insulin drip. "Glyburide each morning as the initial drug" is not the best choice because Glyburide crosses the placenta and is not first-line drug therapy for gestational diabetes. "A confirmatory 100-g glucose tolerance test" is not the best choice because The one-step 75-g test both screens and diagnoses; a second tolerance test is not required. "Postpartum testing with no prenatal therapy" is not the best choice because Antepartum treatment lowers perinatal risk. Postpartum screening is added later, not substituted for prenatal care.

references.label: StatPearls. Gestational diabetes. Initial management is nutrition, activity, and glucose monitoring.

blueprintTopic: Insulin when gestational diabetes escapes diet
vignette: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 31 weeks was diagnosed with gestational diabetes two weeks ago. She has followed a nutrition plan. Home readings on four days show fasting glucose 108 to 118 mg/dL and 1-hour postmeal values 146 to 158 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. She declines no recommended therapy and can use injections.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start glyburide as the preferred first drug
Induce labor this week for the glucose values
Continue diet alone and recheck in four weeks
Add insulin and keep reviewing the meal plan
Start metformin and stop glucose logs
correctAnswer: Add insulin and keep reviewing the meal plan
explanation: Fasting glucose is above the usual target of under 95 mg/dL and postmeal values are above 140 mg/dL at 1 hour. When lifestyle measures are not enough, insulin is the preferred drug because it does not cross the placenta. "Continue diet alone and recheck in four weeks" is not the best choice because Two weeks of readings already above target should not wait another month. "Start glyburide as the preferred first drug" is not the best choice because Glyburide is not first-line; it crosses the placenta and has more neonatal complications than insulin. "Start metformin and stop glucose logs" is not the best choice because Metformin is an alternative only when insulin cannot be used, and monitoring continues. "Induce labor this week for the glucose values" is not the best choice because These readings are a signal to treat, not an indication for delivery at 31 weeks.

references.label: StatPearls. Gestational diabetes. Insulin is first-line when nutrition does not meet glucose targets.

blueprintTopic: Postpartum glucose testing after gestational diabetes
vignette: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, is seen 8 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Gestational diabetes was diet-controlled. She is breastfeeding, feels well, and has no polydipsia. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Fasting capillary glucose at home this week was 94 mg/dL. She asks what testing she still needs.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Hemoglobin A1c on a five-year schedule
Repeat the prenatal 50-g glucose screen
Start insulin because the pregnancy was affected
A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test now
No testing unless symptoms appear
correctAnswer: A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test now
explanation: Guidelines recommend diabetes screening for every woman with gestational diabetes, ideally 4 to 12 weeks after delivery, commonly with a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. A normal fingerstick does not replace that test. "No testing unless symptoms appear" is not the best choice because Many women who progress to diabetes are asymptomatic, so testing is routine. "Hemoglobin A1c on a five-year schedule" is not the best choice because The early postpartum test is a glucose tolerance test. A1c can miss recent hyperglycemia and is not the preferred 4-to-12-week test. "Repeat the prenatal 50-g glucose screen" is not the best choice because The 50-g screen is an antepartum screening step, not the postpartum diagnostic test. "Start insulin because the pregnancy was affected" is not the best choice because Most diet-controlled gestational diabetes resolves after the placenta is delivered. Treatment waits on the postpartum test.

references.label: StatPearls. Gestational diabetes. Postpartum screening is recommended 4 to 12 weeks after delivery.

blueprintTopic: Intrapartum penicillin for a positive GBS culture
vignette: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, is in labor at 39 weeks. A rectovaginal culture at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. She has no drug allergy. Temperature is 37.0 C, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, and pulse 88/min. The cervix is 5 cm dilated and membranes are intact. The fetal heart rate is 142/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Antibiotics after the membranes rupture
Oral amoxicillin after the birth
Intrapartum clindamycin despite no allergy
Intravenous penicillin during labor
Cesarean birth to avoid exposure
correctAnswer: Intravenous penicillin during labor
explanation: A positive antenatal group B streptococcus culture is an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Penicillin is preferred because of its narrow spectrum. It is given during labor, not delayed until rupture of membranes. "Oral amoxicillin after the birth" is not the best choice because Prophylaxis has to reach the fetus before birth. Postpartum oral therapy does not prevent early-onset disease. "Intrapartum clindamycin despite no allergy" is not the best choice because Clindamycin is reserved for high-risk penicillin allergy when the isolate is susceptible. "Cesarean birth to avoid exposure" is not the best choice because Colonization alone is not an indication for cesarean birth. "Antibiotics after the membranes rupture" is not the best choice because Prophylaxis starts in labor. Intact membranes do not cancel a positive culture.

references.label: StatPearls. Group B streptococcus and pregnancy. Penicillin is first-line intrapartum prophylaxis.

blueprintTopic: GBS bacteriuria still requires intrapartum prophylaxis
vignette: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, presents in labor at 39 weeks. At 14 weeks a urine culture grew group B streptococcus at 10,000 CFU/mL and she completed a course of antibiotics. She had no fever then. No 36-week rectovaginal swab was collected. Temperature now is 36.8 C, pulse 90/min, and the cervix is 4 cm. She has no penicillin allergy.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: A rapid culture and antibiotics if it grows
Oral nitrofurantoin until delivery
Cesarean birth because of the old urine culture
Intravenous penicillin during this labor
No antibiotics because the urine infection was treated
correctAnswer: Intravenous penicillin during this labor
explanation: Group B streptococcus bacteriuria at any colony count during pregnancy is evidence of colonization. Intrapartum prophylaxis is indicated even after the bacteriuria itself was treated. Penicillin is the preferred agent. "No antibiotics because the urine infection was treated" is not the best choice because Treating the urinary isolate does not remove the indication for prophylaxis in labor. "A rapid culture and antibiotics if it grows" is not the best choice because The bacteriuria already establishes the indication. Waiting on a new culture misses the intrapartum window. "Oral nitrofurantoin until delivery" is not the best choice because Urinary oral agents do not provide intrapartum prophylaxis. "Cesarean birth because of the old urine culture" is not the best choice because Bacteriuria is an indication for antibiotics in labor, not for cesarean birth.

references.label: StatPearls. Group B streptococcus bacteriuria of any concentration is an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis.

blueprintTopic: Unknown GBS status with prolonged rupture of membranes
vignette: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, arrives in labor at 39 weeks. Her group B streptococcus status was never collected. Membranes ruptured 20 hours ago. Temperature is 37.1 C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, and pulse 92/min. The cervix is 6 cm. She has no drug allergy. The fetal heart rate is 150/min with moderate variability.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intrapartum clindamycin as a default drug
Immediate cesarean birth for the rupture interval
Intravenous penicillin during labor
No antibiotics at term without a positive swab
Antibiotics if she develops a fever
correctAnswer: Intravenous penicillin during labor
explanation: When group B streptococcus status is unknown at 37 weeks or later, prophylaxis is indicated if membranes have been ruptured for 18 hours or more. Penicillin is preferred in the absence of allergy. Fever is a separate indication, not a requirement. "No antibiotics at term without a positive swab" is not the best choice because Unknown status plus prolonged rupture is itself an indication. "Immediate cesarean birth for the rupture interval" is not the best choice because The interval calls for antibiotics, not operative birth, while the tracing is reassuring. "Intrapartum clindamycin as a default drug" is not the best choice because She has no penicillin allergy, so clindamycin is not the first choice. "Antibiotics if she develops a fever" is not the best choice because Fever would also qualify, but 20 hours of ruptured membranes already qualifies.

references.label: StatPearls. Unknown GBS status with rupture of membranes of at least 18 hours is an indication for prophylaxis.

blueprintTopic: No GBS prophylaxis for cesarean without labor
vignette: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, is admitted at 39 weeks for a planned repeat cesarean birth. A 36-week culture grew group B streptococcus. She is not in labor, membranes are intact, and the fetal heart rate is 140/min. Temperature is 36.7 C and blood pressure is 126/80 mm Hg. She has no drug allergy. The surgical team asks about prophylaxis before the incision.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Clindamycin in the operating room by default
Delay the cesarean until she labors
Intravenous penicillin for four hours before incision
A new culture and cancel the operation today
No intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis
correctAnswer: No intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis
explanation: Intrapartum prophylaxis is not needed for cesarean birth when labor has not started and the membranes are intact, even if the antenatal culture was positive. Routine surgical antibiotics are a separate decision and are not group B streptococcus-specific prophylaxis. "Intravenous penicillin for four hours before incision" is not the best choice because That regimen is for labor or ruptured membranes, which are absent here. "Delay the cesarean until she labors" is not the best choice because Waiting for labor would create the exposure the planned cesarean avoids. "Clindamycin in the operating room by default" is not the best choice because She has no high-risk penicillin allergy, and specific prophylaxis is not indicated. "A new culture and cancel the operation today" is not the best choice because The existing culture does not change a planned cesarean with intact membranes and no labor.

references.label: StatPearls. GBS prophylaxis is not indicated for cesarean birth without labor or rupture of membranes.

blueprintTopic: Clindamycin only when the GBS isolate is susceptible
vignette: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, is in labor at 38 weeks. Her 36-week culture grew group B streptococcus. She developed anaphylaxis after penicillin five years ago. The laboratory reported the isolate susceptible to clindamycin, and a D-zone test was negative. Temperature is 37.2 C, pulse 96/min, and the cervix is 7 cm.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Oral azithromycin after delivery
Intravenous clindamycin until delivery
Intravenous penicillin with diphenhydramine
No prophylaxis because of the allergy history
Intravenous vancomycin as the default drug
correctAnswer: Intravenous clindamycin until delivery
explanation: After anaphylaxis, penicillin and cephalosporins are avoided. Clindamycin is appropriate only when the isolate is susceptible to clindamycin and inducible resistance is absent. Both conditions are met here. "Intravenous penicillin with diphenhydramine" is not the best choice because Anaphylaxis is a high-risk allergy. Premedication does not make penicillin safe. "Intravenous vancomycin as the default drug" is not the best choice because Vancomycin is used when the isolate is not known to be clindamycin susceptible. "Oral azithromycin after delivery" is not the best choice because Macrolide therapy after birth does not replace intrapartum prophylaxis. "No prophylaxis because of the allergy history" is not the best choice because Allergy changes the drug. It does not remove the indication.

references.label: StatPearls. Clindamycin is used for high-risk penicillin allergy only if the isolate is susceptible.

blueprintTopic: Cefazolin for a low-risk penicillin allergy
vignette: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, is in labor at 40 weeks. Group B streptococcus culture at 36 weeks was positive. As a child she had a nonurticarial rash on the third day of an oral penicillin course and has since taken amoxicillin without trouble. She describes no anaphylaxis, hives, or breathing trouble. Temperature is 36.9 C and the cervix is 5 cm.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intravenous cefazolin during labor
No prophylaxis because any rash forbids beta-lactams
Intravenous vancomycin during labor
Cesarean birth to avoid antibiotic exposure
Oral clindamycin for five days after birth
correctAnswer: Intravenous cefazolin during labor
explanation: A remote nonurticarial rash is a low-risk penicillin allergy. A first-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin is recommended for intrapartum prophylaxis in that setting. Vancomycin and clindamycin are for high-risk allergy. "Intravenous vancomycin during labor" is not the best choice because Vancomycin is for high-risk allergy without clindamycin susceptibility, which this history is not. "No prophylaxis because any rash forbids beta-lactams" is not the best choice because A low-risk rash does not forbid cefazolin, and prophylaxis is still indicated. "Oral clindamycin for five days after birth" is not the best choice because Postpartum oral therapy does not prevent early-onset neonatal disease. "Cesarean birth to avoid antibiotic exposure" is not the best choice because The allergy history does not change the route of birth.

references.label: StatPearls. Low-risk penicillin allergy is treated with cefazolin for GBS prophylaxis.

blueprintTopic: McRoberts maneuver for shoulder dystocia
vignette: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, is pushing at 39 weeks. The fetal head delivers and then retracts against the perineum. Gentle downward traction does not deliver the anterior shoulder. The fetal heart rate was 140/min before the head delivered. She has an epidural and can still flex her hips. Estimated fetal weight on the last scan was 4100 g.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: More downward traction on the fetal head
Immediate Zavanelli replacement of the head
Stop and move to cesarean with the head delivered
McRoberts flexion with suprapubic pressure
Fundal pressure while she keeps pushing
correctAnswer: McRoberts flexion with suprapubic pressure
explanation: After the head delivers and the shoulder is stuck, the first maneuvers are to call for help, stop extra pushing and traction, flex and abduct the hips (McRoberts), and apply suprapubic pressure. Fundal pressure drives the shoulder into the pubic bone. "Fundal pressure while she keeps pushing" is not the best choice because Fundal pressure worsens impaction of the anterior shoulder and is avoided. "Immediate Zavanelli replacement of the head" is not the best choice because Cephalic replacement is a last-resort maneuver after first- and second-line steps fail. "More downward traction on the fetal head" is not the best choice because Increasing traction raises the risk of brachial plexus injury and does not relieve the bony impaction. "Stop and move to cesarean with the head delivered" is not the best choice because The head is already out. Abdominal delivery is not the next maneuver.

references.label: StatPearls. Shoulder dystocia. First-line management is McRoberts maneuver with suprapubic pressure. Avoid fundal pressure.

blueprintTopic: Tranexamic acid within three hours of birth
vignette: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 1, is bleeding from uterine atony 40 minutes after vaginal birth. Oxytocin is running and bimanual massage is underway. Blood pressure is 100/64 mm Hg and pulse is 118/min. Estimated blood loss is 1100 mL. She has no history of thrombosis. Temperature is 37.0 C.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Pack the vagina and send her home
Give intravenous tranexamic acid now
Withhold tranexamic acid because she is normotensive
Immediate hysterectomy before any further drug
Stop oxytocin and give tranexamic acid tomorrow
correctAnswer: Give intravenous tranexamic acid now
explanation: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously is given within 3 hours of birth once postpartum hemorrhage is diagnosed, together with uterotonic therapy. She is 40 minutes after birth, so the window is open. It does not replace oxytocin. "Stop oxytocin and give tranexamic acid tomorrow" is not the best choice because oxytocin continues, and tomorrow is outside the three-hour window. "Immediate hysterectomy before any further drug" is not the best choice because medical therapy and tamponade come before hysterectomy. "Withhold tranexamic acid because she is normotensive" is not the best choice because the indication is hemorrhage, not hypertension. "Pack the vagina and send her home" is not the best choice because she is tachycardic with ongoing atony and is not stable for discharge.

references.label: StatPearls. Postpartum hemorrhage. Give tranexamic acid within 3 hours of birth, along with uterotonic therapy.

blueprintTopic: Avoid carboprost in asthma
vignette: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 3, has ongoing bleeding from a boggy uterus after vaginal birth. Massage and an oxytocin infusion are in progress. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. She uses an albuterol inhaler for asthma and was wheezing last week. Estimated blood loss is 850 mL. Temperature is 36.9 C.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop massage so the uterus can rest
Immediate hysterectomy as the next step
Intramuscular methylergonovine as the next uterotonic
A fluid bolus alone without another drug
Intramuscular carboprost as the next uterotonic for this patient
correctAnswer: Intramuscular methylergonovine as the next uterotonic
explanation: Carboprost can cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. Her blood pressure is normal, so methylergonovine is an appropriate second uterotonic while oxytocin and massage continue. "Intramuscular carboprost as the next uterotonic for this patient" is not the best choice because Carboprost is avoided in asthma because it can provoke bronchospasm. "Stop massage so the uterus can rest" is not the best choice because Bimanual massage is treatment for atony, not something to stop while bleeding continues. "Immediate hysterectomy as the next step" is not the best choice because A second uterotonic comes before hysterectomy. "A fluid bolus alone without another drug" is not the best choice because Volume replacement supports perfusion but does not contract a boggy uterus.

references.label: StatPearls. Postpartum hemorrhage. Carboprost may cause bronchospasm in asthma. Methylergonovine is relatively contraindicated in hypertension.

blueprintTopic: Parathyroidectomy for osteoporosis in primary hyperparathyroidism
vignette: A 58-year-old woman has a serum calcium of 11.4 mg/dL on two mornings. Parathyroid hormone is 88 pg/mL (reference 15 to 65) and creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. She has no kidney stones and feels well. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Bone density shows a femoral-neck T-score of -2.8. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 32 ng/mL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Cinacalcet and no surgical referral
Referral for parathyroidectomy
Observation because she has no symptoms
Calcitonin injections as long-term therapy
Neck exploration without confirming the labs
correctAnswer: Referral for parathyroidectomy
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is confirmed by high calcium with a PTH that is not suppressed. Surgery is indicated for osteoporosis, defined as a T-score of -2.5 or lower, even when the patient feels well. Localization scans are for operative planning and do not replace the indication. "Observation because she has no symptoms" is not the best choice because Absence of stones or fractures does not cancel a surgical indication once bone density is in the osteoporosis range. "Cinacalcet and no surgical referral" is not the best choice because Calcimimetics are not a substitute for surgery in a patient who meets operative criteria. "Neck exploration without confirming the labs" is not the best choice because The biochemical diagnosis is already made. The next management step is referral for curative surgery, with localization arranged by the surgeon. "Calcitonin injections as long-term therapy" is not the best choice because Calcitonin is not durable treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism.

references.label: StatPearls. Primary hyperparathyroidism. Surgery is indicated for a T-score of -2.5 or lower.

blueprintTopic: Salivary cortisol when an estrogen pill cannot be stopped
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has gained 9 kg, developed wide purple abdominal striae, and has a blood pressure of 158/96 mm Hg. She takes a combined oral contraceptive for contraception and cannot stop it this month. Morning glucose is 118 mg/dL. She does not use glucocorticoid pills or injections. You plan the first test for endogenous hypercortisolism.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Pituitary MRI before any cortisol test
Late-night salivary cortisol while she stays on the pill
A 1-mg dexamethasone test interpreted on serum cortisol for this patient
Adrenal vein sampling as the first study
Morning serum cortisol alone as a rule-out test
correctAnswer: Late-night salivary cortisol while she stays on the pill
explanation: Estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, so tests that measure serum total cortisol, including the dexamethasone suppression test, are unreliable until the pill has been stopped for several weeks. Late-night salivary cortisol reflects free cortisol and is useful when the contraceptive cannot be stopped. "A 1-mg dexamethasone test interpreted on serum cortisol for this patient" is not the best choice because Serum total cortisol is increased by estrogen even when free cortisol is normal, so a positive test would be uninterpretable. "Morning serum cortisol alone as a rule-out test" is not the best choice because A single morning serum cortisol neither confirms nor excludes Cushing syndrome, and estrogen affects the total level. "Pituitary MRI before any cortisol test" is not the best choice because Imaging comes after hypercortisolism and ACTH dependence are shown. "Adrenal vein sampling as the first study" is not the best choice because Venous sampling is not a screening test for Cushing syndrome.

references.label: PMC6080996. Salivary cortisol is useful when oral estrogen cannot be stopped. Serum total cortisol tests should wait until estrogen is stopped.

blueprintTopic: Letrozole for anovulatory PCOS infertility
vignette: A 28-year-old woman and her partner want to conceive. She has oligomenorrhea, acne, and a serum total testosterone of 62 ng/dL. Pelvic ultrasound shows a typical polycystic ovarian pattern. Semen analysis is normal and a hysterosalpingogram last month showed patent tubes. Body mass index is 29 kg/m2. Pregnancy test today is negative. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Letrozole for ovulation induction
Empiric cabergoline for a presumed prolactinoma
Metformin alone and no ovulation drug
Immediate in vitro fertilization
A combined oral contraceptive for six cycles
correctAnswer: Letrozole for ovulation induction
explanation: The 2023 international PCOS guideline recommends letrozole as first-line ovulation induction for infertile anovulatory women with PCOS and no other infertility factor. Pregnancy has been excluded. A contraceptive would prevent the pregnancy she wants. "A combined oral contraceptive for six cycles" is not the best choice because A contraceptive treats cycle control when pregnancy is not desired. It blocks conception. "Immediate in vitro fertilization" is not the best choice because Tubal and semen tests are normal. Ovulation induction comes before assisted reproduction. "Empiric cabergoline for a presumed prolactinoma" is not the best choice because Nothing in the history suggests hyperprolactinemia, and the drug was not indicated by a prolactin level. "Metformin alone and no ovulation drug" is not the best choice because Metformin can be used, but the guideline states letrozole is more effective first-line ovulation therapy.

references.label: 2023 international PCOS guideline (PMC10477934). Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction for anovulatory infertility.

blueprintTopic: Uterine evacuation for a complete hydatidiform mole
vignette: A 22-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, has had vaginal bleeding for six days at 11 weeks by dates. The uterus is the size of 16 weeks. Serum beta-hCG is 240,000 mIU/mL. Ultrasound shows a uterus filled with cystic spaces and no embryo. Blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg and pulse is 104/min. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. Chest radiograph is clear. She wants future fertility.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Multiagent chemotherapy before any uterine procedure
Dilation and evacuation delayed until after 20 weeks
Hysterectomy as the required first treatment
Suction uterine evacuation and serial beta-hCG
Expectant care and a repeat ultrasound in two weeks
correctAnswer: Suction uterine evacuation and serial beta-hCG
explanation: A complete mole is diagnosed by bleeding, a large uterus, markedly elevated beta-hCG, and a cystic ultrasound pattern. Most moles resolve after uterine evacuation. Serial beta-hCG then detects the minority that become gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Fertility-sparing evacuation is appropriate. "Multiagent chemotherapy before any uterine procedure" is not the best choice because Chemotherapy is for neoplasia that persists after evacuation, not the first step for an apparent mole. "Hysterectomy as the required first treatment" is not the best choice because Hysterectomy is not required for a young patient who wants fertility. "Expectant care and a repeat ultrasound in two weeks" is not the best choice because A symptomatic mole with a markedly elevated beta-hCG is not observed. "Dilation and evacuation delayed until after 20 weeks" is not the best choice because Evacuation is not postponed into the second half of pregnancy.

references.label: PMC9978730. Hydatidiform mole is treated by uterine evacuation, then serial hCG monitoring.

blueprintTopic: Aldosterone-renin ratio before adrenal imaging
vignette: A 46-year-old man has blood pressures of 162/98 mm Hg on amlodipine, lisinopril, and chlorthalidone. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. He is not taking spironolactone. He has no paroxysmal headache, palpitations, or sweating. You plan the evaluation for primary aldosteronism.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Plasma metanephrines as the endocrine test
Adrenal CT as the first test
Empiric spironolactone without measuring renin
Morning aldosterone and renin after potassium is corrected
Renal-artery duplex because the potassium is low for this patient
correctAnswer: Morning aldosterone and renin after potassium is corrected
explanation: The Endocrine Society suggests screening hypertension with a morning aldosterone and renin and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Hypokalemia can falsely lower aldosterone, so potassium is corrected and the ratio is repeated if the first screen is negative. Imaging is not the screening test. "Adrenal CT as the first test" is not the best choice because An incidental adenoma is common. Biochemical screening comes before imaging. "Empiric spironolactone without measuring renin" is not the best choice because Treatment without confirming renin suppression misses other causes of hypokalemic hypertension. "Plasma metanephrines as the endocrine test" is not the best choice because He has no spells to suggest pheochromocytoma. Metanephrines do not diagnose aldosteronism. "Renal-artery duplex because the potassium is low for this patient" is not the best choice because Renovascular hypertension raises renin. Suppressed renin with a relatively high aldosterone points the other way and is tested with the ratio.

references.label: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism guideline. Screen with aldosterone and renin. Correct hypokalemia because it can falsely lower aldosterone.

blueprintTopic: Endometrial sampling when the stripe is thick
vignette: A 61-year-old woman has had one episode of vaginal bleeding eight years after her last period. She takes no estrogen. Blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Hemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial stripe of 12 mm and no adnexal mass. Pregnancy test is negative.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pills for three months
Cervical conization as the first procedure
Hysterectomy without a tissue diagnosis
Office endometrial biopsy
Reassurance and a repeat examination in one year
correctAnswer: Office endometrial biopsy
explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding with an endometrial thickness of 12 mm needs tissue sampling. An endometrial biopsy is the appropriate next step. Thickness above 4 mm, or persistent bleeding, is not followed by reassurance. "Reassurance and a repeat examination in one year" is not the best choice because Bleeding after menopause is evaluated now. A thick stripe raises concern for hyperplasia or cancer. "Combined oral contraceptive pills for three months" is not the best choice because Hormonal suppression does not diagnose the cause of postmenopausal bleeding. "Hysterectomy without a tissue diagnosis" is not the best choice because Surgery may follow a biopsy result. It is not the first step. "Cervical conization as the first procedure" is not the best choice because The ultrasound abnormality is endometrial, not a cervical lesion that needs conization.

references.label: StatPearls. Postmenopausal bleeding. A thick endometrial stripe is evaluated with tissue sampling.

blueprintTopic: TSH before treating a thyroid nodule in pregnancy
vignette: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 18 weeks has a newly felt right thyroid nodule. Ultrasound shows a solid 2.3-cm nodule and no abnormal nodes. She reports heat intolerance. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 128/70 mm Hg. No TSH has been drawn. Fetal heart rate is 150/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Total thyroidectomy this week without labs
Defer evaluation until after delivery
Measure a serum TSH before any invasive step
Empiric methimazole and no laboratory test
Radioiodine ablation during this trimester for this patient
correctAnswer: Measure a serum TSH before any invasive step
explanation: In pregnancy, a thyroid nodule is evaluated with ultrasound and a TSH. TSH is measured to detect a toxic adenoma before decisions about aspiration or surgery. Fine-needle aspiration, when indicated, is safe in pregnancy. Radioiodine and empiric drugs are not the first step. "Radioiodine ablation during this trimester for this patient" is not the best choice because Radioiodine is not a first test or treatment of an uncharacterized nodule in pregnancy. "Total thyroidectomy this week without labs" is not the best choice because Differentiated cancer, once proven, can often wait until after delivery. Surgery is not the first step before TSH. "Empiric methimazole and no laboratory test" is not the best choice because Antithyroid drug requires a diagnosis of hyperthyroidism, which starts with TSH. "Defer evaluation until after delivery" is not the best choice because A 2.3-cm nodule is evaluated during pregnancy. It is not ignored until postpartum.

references.label: StatPearls. Thyroid disease and pregnancy. Women with thyroid nodules need a TSH, and aspiration indications match those outside pregnancy.

blueprintTopic: Surgery when calcium exceeds the limit by 1 mg/dL
vignette: A 66-year-old man has serum calcium of 12.1 mg/dL on two mornings. The laboratory upper limit is 10.2 mg/dL. Parathyroid hormone is 95 pg/mL and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. He has no stones. Femoral-neck T-score is -1.1. Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 36 ng/mL. He feels well and asks whether an operation is indicated.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Observation because the T-score is better than -2.5
Sestamibi scan alone and no operation
Long-term calcitonin as sole therapy
Referral for parathyroidectomy
Bisphosphonate therapy and no surgical referral
correctAnswer: Referral for parathyroidectomy
explanation: Calcium of 12.1 mg/dL is more than 1.0 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal. That degree of hypercalcemia is an indication for parathyroidectomy in primary hyperparathyroidism even when bone density is not osteoporotic and the patient feels well. "Observation because the T-score is better than -2.5" is not the best choice because Osteoporosis is one indication. Marked hypercalcemia is another, and it is already met. "Long-term calcitonin as sole therapy" is not the best choice because Calcitonin does not cure primary hyperparathyroidism. "Bisphosphonate therapy and no surgical referral" is not the best choice because A bisphosphonate does not replace surgery when an operative indication is present. "Sestamibi scan alone and no operation" is not the best choice because A localization scan plans the operation. It is not an alternative to referral.

references.label: StatPearls. Primary hyperparathyroidism. Surgery is indicated when calcium is more than 1.0 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal.

blueprintTopic: Capacity despite a dementia diagnosis
vignette: A 78-year-old man with mild dementia is offered appendectomy for imaging-confirmed appendicitis. He states the operation, the risk of death and of rupture if he declines, and the antibiotic alternative. He chooses surgery and repeats that choice an hour later. Temperature is 38.1 C and pulse is 96/min. A note from last year says he needs help with bills.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Give antibiotics because consent is impossible
Refuse the operation because of the dementia label
Accept his consent and proceed to surgery
Let his adult daughter decide over his objection
Ask a judge to declare him incompetent first
correctAnswer: Accept his consent and proceed to surgery
explanation: A dementia diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity. He understands the operation, appreciates the risk, gives reasons, and states a stable choice. That is capacity for this decision, so his consent is valid. "Ask a judge to declare him incompetent first" is not the best choice because Competence is a court finding. It is not required when the bedside assessment shows capacity. "Refuse the operation because of the dementia label" is not the best choice because The label is not a capacity determination. "Let his adult daughter decide over his objection" is not the best choice because A surrogate is used when the patient lacks capacity, which he has not been shown to lack. "Give antibiotics because consent is impossible" is not the best choice because Consent is possible here, and antibiotics alone are not the indicated treatment he accepted.

references.label: StatPearls. Competency and capacity. Dementia does not automatically remove decision-making capacity.

blueprintTopic: Reassess capacity after intoxication
vignette: A 44-year-old man with a blood alcohol level of 280 mg/dL refuses laparotomy for free air under the diaphragm. He cannot name the operation or the risk of death. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. No surrogate is present. He keeps trying to leave the stretcher.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Wait for a court hearing before any operation for this patient
Honor the refusal and discharge him now
Give oral antibiotics and send him home
Ask the nurse to sign the consent form
Treat under emergency exception and reassess later
correctAnswer: Treat under emergency exception and reassess later
explanation: He cannot understand or reason about a life-threatening decision, and delay for a court hearing would cause serious harm. Emergency treatment proceeds. Capacity is reassessed when he is sober because intoxication is temporary. "Honor the refusal and discharge him now" is not the best choice because A refusal is valid only if the patient has capacity. He cannot show that. "Wait for a court hearing before any operation for this patient" is not the best choice because Perforation will not wait for a hearing. "Ask the nurse to sign the consent form" is not the best choice because Staff cannot consent for a patient. "Give oral antibiotics and send him home" is not the best choice because Free air with hypotension needs source control, not outpatient pills.

references.label: StatPearls. Capacity is decision- and time-specific. Intoxication can temporarily remove it.

blueprintTopic: Capacity is decision-specific
vignette: A 70-year-old man has a court-appointed conservator for his finances. He is admitted with symptomatic cholelithiasis. He describes the operation, the risk of bile leak and of recurrent pain if he declines, and chooses surgery. He gives the same answer after the risks are restated. Blood pressure is 136/78 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Cancel surgery because a conservator exists
Proceed with surgery and skip the discussion
Accept his consent for this operation
Require the financial conservator to consent
Ask the court to approve each medical decision
correctAnswer: Accept his consent for this operation
explanation: Capacity is specific to the decision. A financial conservatorship does not prove he lacks capacity for an operation. He has demonstrated understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and a choice. "Require the financial conservator to consent" is not the best choice because The conservator manages money, not this medical decision, while he retains capacity. "Cancel surgery because a conservator exists" is not the best choice because The legal arrangement is not a medical contraindication. "Ask the court to approve each medical decision" is not the best choice because A new hearing is unnecessary when capacity for this decision is present. "Proceed with surgery and skip the discussion" is not the best choice because The discussion is what established capacity. Skipping it would make consent empty.

references.label: StatPearls. Capacity applies to the decision at hand. A dementia or legal label does not transfer automatically.

blueprintTopic: Consent includes reasonable alternatives
vignette: A 55-year-old woman is asked to sign a consent for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The surgeon described the steps and the risk of bile-duct injury. He did not mention observation, medications for biliary colic, or open surgery. She says she feels rushed. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and pulse is 74/min. Her pain today is 2 out of 10.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discuss reasonable alternatives before she signs
Have a clerk list the alternatives on a form
Cancel the operation because she asked a question
Accept the signature as complete consent
Proceed tonight because the pain score is low
correctAnswer: Discuss reasonable alternatives before she signs
explanation: Informed consent includes the nature of the procedure, risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives, including the risks of those alternatives. A signature without that discussion is not informed consent. "Accept the signature as complete consent" is not the best choice because A signature does not repair a missing element of the discussion. "Have a clerk list the alternatives on a form" is not the best choice because The clinician doing the procedure is responsible for the discussion. "Cancel the operation because she asked a question" is not the best choice because Questions are part of consent, not a reason to cancel an elective case. "Proceed tonight because the pain score is low" is not the best choice because Low pain means the case can wait for a complete discussion. It is not a reason to skip it.

references.label: StatPearls. Informed consent includes the procedure, risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives.

blueprintTopic: Parental permission for a minor
vignette: A 12-year-old boy needs incision and drainage of a forearm abscess. He lives with his mother, is not married, and is not emancipated under state law. He says he wants the procedure. His mother is in the waiting room and has not been spoken with. Temperature is 38.2 C and pulse is 100/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Proceed with no permission because he agreed
Delay care until he turns 18
Obtain his mother's informed permission
Ask a classmate in the lobby to consent
Accept his signature as full legal consent
correctAnswer: Obtain his mother's informed permission
explanation: Children generally cannot give informed consent. A parent or guardian gives informed permission. He can assent, but assent does not replace his mother's permission. He is not emancipated. "Accept his signature as full legal consent" is not the best choice because His agreement is assent, not legal consent. "Ask a classmate in the lobby to consent" is not the best choice because A minor friend has no authority to permit treatment. "Proceed with no permission because he agreed" is not the best choice because Agreement from the child does not replace parental permission for this non-emergency. "Delay care until he turns 18" is not the best choice because The abscess needs treatment now. The missing step is parental permission, not a six-year delay.

references.label: StatPearls. Informed consent. Parents give permission for children who are not emancipated.

blueprintTopic: Emancipated minor may consent
vignette: A 17-year-old woman who is married requests removal of an inflamed appendix. State law in this vignette treats marriage as emancipation. She describes the operation, the risk of perforation, and the antibiotic alternative, and she chooses surgery. Her mother, who disagrees, demands to cancel it. Temperature is 38.3 C and pulse is 104/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Follow the mother's refusal
Accept the patient's consent and proceed
Treat if both mother and patient agree
Discharge her because she is under 18
Wait for a juvenile-court order tonight for this patient
correctAnswer: Accept the patient's consent and proceed
explanation: An emancipated minor may consent. Marriage is a recognized path to emancipation where state law says so, and this stem states that rule. She has capacity for the decision. Her mother's objection does not override it. "Follow the mother's refusal" is not the best choice because Parental refusal does not control once the minor is emancipated and has capacity. "Wait for a juvenile-court order tonight for this patient" is not the best choice because No hearing is required for an emancipated patient who consents. "Treat if both mother and patient agree" is not the best choice because Dual permission is not required. "Discharge her because she is under 18" is not the best choice because Age alone does not block care she can legally accept.

references.label: StatPearls. Informed consent. Married minors are an example of emancipation and may consent.

blueprintTopic: Respect a capacitated refusal of transfusion
vignette: A 58-year-old woman who is a Jehovah's Witness is scheduled for elective hip replacement. Hemoglobin is 13.1 g/dL. She understands she could die if she bleeds and still refuses all blood products. She repeats the refusal after the risks are restated. Blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg and pulse is 72/min. She asks you to record the refusal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Transfuse two units the night before anyway
Cancel the discussion and ask her spouse to consent
Document the refusal and plan surgery without blood
Declare her incompetent because of the refusal
Refuse to operate and end the relationship today
correctAnswer: Document the refusal and plan surgery without blood
explanation: A capacitated adult may refuse transfusion, including for religious reasons, after understanding the risk of death. The refusal is documented and the operation is planned with blood-conservation measures. Disagreement with her choice is not incapacity. "Transfuse two units the night before anyway" is not the best choice because Transfusion over a valid refusal is a battery. "Cancel the discussion and ask her spouse to consent" is not the best choice because A spouse does not override a capacitated patient. "Declare her incompetent because of the refusal" is not the best choice because An unpopular choice is not evidence of incapacity. "Refuse to operate and end the relationship today" is not the best choice because The ethical step is to accommodate a valid refusal, not to abandon her at the first refusal.

references.label: StatPearls. Refusal of care. A capacitated patient may refuse treatment after the risks are understood.

blueprintTopic: Informed refusal when leaving against advice
vignette: A 49-year-old man with chest pressure wants to leave the emergency department before troponin results. He can explain that he may be having a heart attack and that he could die at home. He still chooses to leave and does not appear intoxicated. Blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg and pulse is 92/min. ECG shows no ST-segment elevation.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge him with no discussion of risk
Sedate him and send the blood tests
Explain the risks, document, and allow him to leave
Restrain him until both troponin tests return
Have security sign a hold without assessing capacity
correctAnswer: Explain the risks, document, and allow him to leave
explanation: He has capacity and is refusing further care. The clinician explains the risks, answers questions, documents the informed refusal, offers return precautions, and lets him leave. Restraint requires a lack of capacity or another lawful hold, which is not present. "Restrain him until both troponin tests return" is not the best choice because Restraint of a capacitated patient is not justified by clinician worry. "Have security sign a hold without assessing capacity" is not the best choice because Security staff cannot create a medical hold. "Discharge him with no discussion of risk" is not the best choice because Leaving is allowed. Skipping the risk discussion is not informed refusal. "Sedate him and send the blood tests" is not the best choice because Chemical restraint is not a substitute for respecting a capacitated refusal.

references.label: StatPearls. Refusal of care. Determine capacity, explain risks, and respect a capacitated refusal.

blueprintTopic: Report suspected child abuse
vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a swollen thigh. Radiographs show a femur fracture and two older rib fractures. His mother says he fell off a couch yesterday and asks you not to call anyone. He is quiet and has bruises of different colors on his back. Temperature is 37.0 C and pulse is 120/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Wait for the mother to agree to a report
Report the suspicion to child protective services
Tell the family pastor
Document bruises and make no report
Discharge if she signs that the fall happened for this patient
correctAnswer: Report the suspicion to child protective services
explanation: Suspicion of child abuse must be reported. Certainty is not required, and a parent's request not to call does not cancel the duty. The fracture pattern and bruises of different ages are enough to report. "Wait for the mother to agree to a report" is not the best choice because The duty does not depend on parental permission. "Discharge if she signs that the fall happened for this patient" is not the best choice because A signed story does not explain rib fractures of different ages. "Tell the family pastor" is not the best choice because Clergy notification is not the mandated report to protective services. "Document bruises and make no report" is not the best choice because The chart note does not replace the report.

references.label: StatPearls. Mandatory reporting. Suspected child abuse is reported even without certainty or parental agreement.

blueprintTopic: Report a contagious disease to public health
vignette: A 19-year-old college student has fever, cough, and a morbilliform rash. Measles PCR from the throat is positive. He asks you not to tell the health department because he does not want his dorm notified. Temperature is 38.9 C and pulse is 108/min. He is hypoxic to 94 percent on room air and is being admitted.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Ask the dorm to handle notification instead
Report the case to the health department
Keep the result out of outside notices
Wait until he signs a release
Tell his roommate and no agency
correctAnswer: Report the case to the health department
explanation: Clinicians must report specified communicable diseases to public health authorities. The patient's wish to avoid notice does not cancel that duty. Treatment and isolation still proceed. "Keep the result out of outside notices" is not the best choice because Withholding a reportable infection leaves contacts unwarned. "Tell his roommate and no agency" is not the best choice because A roommate is not the public health authority. "Wait until he signs a release" is not the best choice because This report does not require his authorization. "Ask the dorm to handle notification instead" is not the best choice because The clinician's duty is to the health department, not to delegate the legal report.

references.label: StatPearls. Mandatory reporting includes designated infectious diseases as well as abuse.

blueprintTopic: Report suspected elder abuse
vignette: An 84-year-old woman is admitted with dehydration. Her niece, who controls her accounts, will not say where her pension goes. The patient has a stage 3 sacral ulcer, an empty refrigerator was described by the medic, and she whispers that she is not allowed to phone her son. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg and sodium is 152 mEq/L. Your state designates physicians as mandated reporters of elder abuse.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Ask the niece for permission before any report for this patient
Discharge her back to the niece tonight
Document the ulcer and make no report
Confront the niece and then close the chart
Report the concern to adult protective services
correctAnswer: Report the concern to adult protective services
explanation: Where physicians are mandated reporters, suspected elder neglect and financial abuse is reported. Certainty and the caregiver's permission are not required. The ulcer, isolation, and missing funds are enough to report while she is treated. "Ask the niece for permission before any report for this patient" is not the best choice because The suspected abuser does not control whether a mandated report is made. "Document the ulcer and make no report" is not the best choice because A chart note is not the report the statute requires. "Confront the niece and then close the chart" is not the best choice because A confrontation without a report leaves her unprotected. "Discharge her back to the niece tonight" is not the best choice because Sending her back before reporting and a safe plan continues the risk.

references.label: StatPearls. Mandatory reporting laws generally cover elder abuse, and the duty follows state law.

blueprintTopic: On-call physician may not refuse for lack of insurance
vignette: A 40-year-old man without insurance has right-lower-quadrant pain, fever of 38.4 C, and a CT scan showing appendicitis. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. The on-call surgeon says he does not treat uninsured patients and will not come to the emergency department.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Require the on-call surgeon to evaluate him
Transfer him before any further care
Discharge him to find a surgeon tomorrow
Schedule an elective operation next month
Delay the examination until a deposit is paid
correctAnswer: Require the on-call surgeon to evaluate him
explanation: EMTALA requires on-call physicians to help evaluate and stabilize an emergency condition without regard to insurance or ability to pay. Appendicitis on CT is an emergency. The surgeon does not get to decline because the patient is uninsured. "Discharge him to find a surgeon tomorrow" is not the best choice because an emergency condition is not sent out untreated. "Delay the examination until a deposit is paid" is not the best choice because payment questions cannot delay screening or stabilizing care. "Transfer him before any further care" is not the best choice because an unstable or unstabilized emergency is not transferred for financial reasons. "Schedule an elective operation next month" is not the best choice because appendicitis is not an elective next-month problem.

references.label: StatPearls. EMTALA and patient transfers. On-call physicians may not refuse to treat an emergency because of insurance status.

blueprintTopic: Follow a valid living will
vignette: A 79-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer is unconscious from a large intracranial bleed. Two physicians have documented that she is terminally ill. Her living will refuses intubation and mechanical ventilation. Her daughter demands intubation. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 88 percent on a nonrebreather mask.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intubate and withdraw the tube if the daughter agrees later
Follow the living will and do not intubate
Ask the ethics committee before honoring the will
Intubate because the daughter is at the bedside
Provide ventilation because oxygen saturation is low
correctAnswer: Follow the living will and do not intubate
explanation: A living will is the patient's prior autonomous refusal. When she lacks capacity and the document applies, it is followed. A daughter's demand does not override it. Comfort measures continue. "Intubate because the daughter is at the bedside" is not the best choice because The surrogate does not replace a clear directive that covers this decision. "Intubate and withdraw the tube if the daughter agrees later" is not the best choice because Starting a refused intervention to negotiate later violates the directive. "Ask the ethics committee before honoring the will" is not the best choice because A clear, applicable directive does not need a committee to be valid. "Provide ventilation because oxygen saturation is low" is not the best choice because Hypoxemia does not erase a refusal of ventilation.

references.label: StatPearls. Advance directives. A living will is followed when the patient lacks capacity.

blueprintTopic: Substituted judgment by the surrogate
vignette: A 68-year-old man is unconscious after a large ischemic stroke. He has no written directive. He named his brother as health care proxy. The brother says, Doctor, what would you do if this were your father? The patient had told friends he would not want a feeding tube if he could not speak. Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Order a feeding tube because you would want one
Wait for a different relative who wants more treatment
Tell the brother to pick what the brother wants
Ask what the patient himself would have chosen
Ask the nurse to choose the plan
correctAnswer: Ask what the patient himself would have chosen
explanation: A health care proxy uses substituted judgment: the choice the patient would have made, based on his known values. The brother's preferences and the clinician's preferences are not the standard. "Tell the brother to pick what the brother wants" is not the best choice because That is the surrogate's preference, not substituted judgment. "Order a feeding tube because you would want one" is not the best choice because The clinician's personal wish is not the patient's wish. "Ask the nurse to choose the plan" is not the best choice because The named proxy is the decision-maker. "Wait for a different relative who wants more treatment" is not the best choice because A different relative does not outrank the named proxy.

references.label: StatPearls. Advance directives. Substituted judgment means choosing what the patient would have wanted.

blueprintTopic: Do not override a valid DNR
vignette: An 86-year-old woman with a signed do-not-resuscitate order becomes pulseless on the medical ward. The order is in the chart and was confirmed with her yesterday, when she had capacity. Her son arrives and shouts for chest compressions. The monitor shows asystole. A nurse asks whether to start CPR.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Call security to make the son decide
Intubate but withhold compressions
Do not start chest compressions
Begin CPR because the son demands it
Start CPR for two minutes and then stop
correctAnswer: Do not start chest compressions
explanation: A do-not-resuscitate order is a refusal of resuscitative efforts. It remains in force. A relative's demand during the arrest does not cancel an order the patient confirmed while she had capacity. "Begin CPR because the son demands it" is not the best choice because The son cannot override her order. "Start CPR for two minutes and then stop" is not the best choice because A brief code is still resuscitation she refused. "Call security to make the son decide" is not the best choice because Security does not adjudicate a valid order. "Intubate but withhold compressions" is not the best choice because Intubation for arrest is part of the resuscitation she declined.

references.label: StatPearls. Advance directives. A DNR order refuses resuscitative efforts and is followed.

blueprintTopic: A capacitated patient can revoke a DNR
vignette: A 74-year-old man with a do-not-resuscitate order from last year is awake and oriented. He is about to undergo elective hernia repair. He says he wants full resuscitation during this admission and explains what CPR and ventilation are. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min. His daughter prefers the old order.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Keep the old order because it cannot be changed
Keep the old order because his daughter prefers it
Suspend the discussion until after the operation
Ask the surgeon to decide during induction
Cancel the DNR for this admission at his request
correctAnswer: Cancel the DNR for this admission at his request
explanation: While he has capacity, his current choice controls. He understands resuscitation and wants it. The old order is revoked or suspended for this admission. A daughter's preference does not keep it in force. "Keep the old order because his daughter prefers it" is not the best choice because She is not the decision-maker while he has capacity. "Keep the old order because it cannot be changed" is not the best choice because Directives can be changed by a capacitated patient. "Ask the surgeon to decide during induction" is not the best choice because The patient already decided. Anesthesia is the wrong moment to rediscover that. "Suspend the discussion until after the operation" is not the best choice because The perioperative plan has to be clear before induction.

references.label: StatPearls. Advance directives. A patient with capacity keeps authority over treatment choices, including resuscitation.

blueprintTopic: Best interest when no surrogate exists
vignette: A 57-year-old man is unconscious after a witnessed collapse. CT shows a ruptured spleen and free blood. Blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg and pulse is 132/min. He has no identification, no directive, and no one who knows him. The surgeon says delay will be fatal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Observe in the ICU without transfusion or surgery
Discharge if blood pressure rises above 90
Take him to surgery in his best interest
Wait until a relative is found
Ask the house supervisor to sign as proxy
correctAnswer: Take him to surgery in his best interest
explanation: When no surrogate and no directive exist, clinicians act in the patient's best interest. Emergency laparotomy for hemorrhagic shock is that action. Waiting for an unknown relative is not safe. "Wait until a relative is found" is not the best choice because He may die during the search. "Observe in the ICU without transfusion or surgery" is not the best choice because Observation does not stop intraperitoneal bleeding. "Ask the house supervisor to sign as proxy" is not the best choice because An administrator is not his surrogate. "Discharge if blood pressure rises above 90" is not the best choice because A transient rise does not treat a ruptured spleen.

references.label: StatPearls. Advance directives. With no surrogate, clinicians act in the patient's best interest.

blueprintTopic: Stabilize before an EMTALA transfer
vignette: A 48-year-old man with hematemesis has a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg and a pulse of 128/min. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL. He is uninsured. The emergency physician has not started fluids or blood. An administrator asks to transfer him to the county hospital before any treatment because of the bill.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Move him to the sidewalk so the duty ends
Discharge him to a clinic in the morning
Transfer now so the receiving hospital can treat for this patient
Start resuscitation and stabilize before any transfer
Ask him to pay before the screening examination
correctAnswer: Start resuscitation and stabilize before any transfer
explanation: EMTALA requires a screening examination and stabilizing treatment of an emergency condition before transfer. Inability to pay does not cancel that duty. Transfer of an unstable patient is allowed only when the benefits outweigh the risks and the receiving hospital accepts him. "Transfer now so the receiving hospital can treat for this patient" is not the best choice because Transfer while he is in shock, before stabilization is attempted, violates the duty. "Discharge him to a clinic in the morning" is not the best choice because Hematemesis with shock is an emergency, not a clinic visit. "Ask him to pay before the screening examination" is not the best choice because The screening examination does not depend on payment. "Move him to the sidewalk so the duty ends" is not the best choice because Moving him off the property to avoid the duty is a violation, not a plan.

references.label: StatPearls. EMTALA and patient transfers. An emergency condition must be stabilized before transfer, regardless of ability to pay.

blueprintTopic: Do not delay the screening exam to ask about payment
vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with chest pressure and sweating. Pulse is 110/min and blood pressure is 154/92 mm Hg. The registrar tells you to collect insurance information and a copay before any clinician examines her.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Send her to a clinic because payment is pending
Examine her before any payment questions
Ask her to leave if she cannot pay tonight
Collect the copay and then decide on an exam
Wait for an insurance authorization number
correctAnswer: Examine her before any payment questions
explanation: EMTALA requires a medical screening examination for anyone who comes to the emergency department seeking care. That examination cannot be delayed to obtain insurance information or to ask about ability to pay. Her vital signs make a cardiac emergency possible. "Collect the copay and then decide on an exam" is not the best choice because payment cannot come before the screening examination. "Send her to a clinic because payment is pending" is not the best choice because a possible emergency is screened here, not redirected for a bill. "Ask her to leave if she cannot pay tonight" is not the best choice because inability to pay does not remove the duty to screen. "Wait for an insurance authorization number" is not the best choice because authorization is not a prerequisite for the screening examination.

references.label: StatPearls. EMTALA and patient transfers. The medical screening examination cannot be delayed to ask about insurance or ability to pay.

blueprintTopic: Teach-back before the consent is complete
vignette: A 60-year-old man is consented for cardiac catheterization. After the explanation he cannot say what procedure is planned or name any risk. He nods when asked if he agrees. Blood pressure is 146/84 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min. The case is elective and scheduled for tomorrow morning.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Cancel catheterization forever
Have him sign and wheel him in now
Repeat the explanation in plain language and teach back
Accept the nod as complete consent
Ask a family member to sign instead for this patient today
correctAnswer: Repeat the explanation in plain language and teach back
explanation: Consent is a communication process. If he cannot restate the procedure or a risk, he has not yet understood it. The explanation is repeated in ordinary language, and teach-back is used before a signature is treated as informed. "Accept the nod as complete consent" is not the best choice because A nod without understanding is not informed consent. "Have him sign and wheel him in now" is not the best choice because The case is elective. There is time to complete the discussion. "Cancel catheterization forever" is not the best choice because Incomplete understanding calls for a better explanation, not permanent cancellation. "Ask a family member to sign instead for this patient today" is not the best choice because He has not been shown to lack capacity. The next step is a clearer discussion with him.

references.label: StatPearls. Informed consent. Teach-back checks whether the patient understood risks, benefits, and alternatives.

blueprintTopic: Thumb spica for a Bennett fracture
vignette: A 26-year-old man punched a wall and has pain at the base of the thumb. Radiographs show an intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal. The thumb is neurovascularly intact. Pulse is 78/min. He can still move the thumb tip.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: A short-arm thumb spica splint
Reassurance and no immobilization
Buddy taping to the index finger
Immediate amputation of the thumb ray
A wrist splint that leaves the thumb free
correctAnswer: A short-arm thumb spica splint
explanation: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture of the first metacarpal base. A short-arm thumb spica splint is appropriate immobilization for first-metacarpal fractures of this type. The thumb has to be included. "Buddy taping to the index finger" is not the best choice because buddy taping does not immobilize the metacarpal base. "A wrist splint that leaves the thumb free" is not the best choice because the thumb must be included in the splint. "Immediate amputation of the thumb ray" is not the best choice because a fracture is immobilized or repaired, not amputated. "Reassurance and no immobilization" is not the best choice because an intra-articular thumb metacarpal fracture is not left unsupported.

references.label: StatPearls. Thumb spica splinting. A short-arm thumb spica is used for first-metacarpal fractures such as Bennett fractures.

blueprintTopic: Aspirate a hot joint before antibiotics
vignette: A 64-year-old man with diabetes has 18 hours of a hot, swollen right knee. He is febrile to 38.6 C, pulse 104/min, and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. He can cooperate with a bedside aspiration. No antibiotics have been given. Glucose is 186 mg/dL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Ice, rest, and a repeat examination tomorrow
Oral cephalexin and clinic follow-up in a week
Colchicine for presumed gout without a tap
Aspirate the knee, then start antibiotics
Start vancomycin and skip aspiration
correctAnswer: Aspirate the knee, then start antibiotics
explanation: A hot native joint is aspirated before antibiotics when the tap can be done promptly. Synovial fluid cell count, crystals, Gram stain, and culture guide therapy. Antibiotics start after the cultures are obtained. "Start vancomycin and skip aspiration" is not the best choice because Antibiotics before the tap can sterilize the only sample that confirms the organism. "Oral cephalexin and clinic follow-up in a week" is not the best choice because Septic arthritis is not an outpatient oral-antibiotic diagnosis. "Colchicine for presumed gout without a tap" is not the best choice because Gout and infection look alike. Crystals do not rule out infection until the fluid is examined. "Ice, rest, and a repeat examination tomorrow" is not the best choice because Delay risks cartilage destruction.

references.label: StatPearls. Septic arthritis. Aspirate the joint, then start empiric antibiotics.

blueprintTopic: Prosthetic joint fluid thresholds are lower
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with a left total knee replacement has had swelling and pain for two days. Temperature is 38.3 C and pulse is 100/min. Synovial fluid shows 18,000 white cells/uL with 82 percent neutrophils. Gram stain is negative. She has no crystals. Blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Repeat the tap in two weeks if pain remains
Treat as prosthetic joint infection after cultures
Reassure her because the count is under 50,000 for this patient
Oral anti-inflammatory drug and no antibiotics
Start colchicine for crystal disease
correctAnswer: Treat as prosthetic joint infection after cultures
explanation: A prosthetic knee does not use the 50,000-cell threshold of a native joint. Fluid with a few thousand white cells and a neutrophil predominance can be infection. She needs surgical consultation, cultures, and antibiotics rather than reassurance. "Reassure her because the count is under 50,000 for this patient" is not the best choice because That threshold is for native joints. It misses prosthetic infection. "Start colchicine for crystal disease" is not the best choice because No crystals were seen, and fever plus a neutrophil-rich fluid is not treated as gout. "Repeat the tap in two weeks if pain remains" is not the best choice because A two-week delay risks implant loss. "Oral anti-inflammatory drug and no antibiotics" is not the best choice because An anti-inflammatory drug does not treat prosthetic infection.

references.label: StatPearls. Septic arthritis. Prosthetic joints use a much lower synovial white-cell threshold.

blueprintTopic: Fasciotomy for compartment syndrome
vignette: A 28-year-old man has severe calf pain six hours after a tibial fracture was splinted. Pain is worse with passive stretch of the toes. The calf is tense. Pulses are present. He received morphine 6 mg without relief. Blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg and pulse is 110/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge if the pulse remains palpable
Observation and a pressure check tomorrow
Emergent fasciotomy
Heparin infusion for arterial thrombus
Elevation and another dose of morphine
correctAnswer: Emergent fasciotomy
explanation: Pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, and a tense compartment are compartment syndrome. It is a clinical diagnosis. Pulses are often still present. The treatment is fasciotomy, not more analgesia. "Elevation and another dose of morphine" is not the best choice because Analgesia and elevation do not decompress the compartment. "Discharge if the pulse remains palpable" is not the best choice because A palpable pulse does not exclude the diagnosis. "Heparin infusion for arterial thrombus" is not the best choice because This is a pressure problem inside a closed compartment, not a primary arterial clot. "Observation and a pressure check tomorrow" is not the best choice because Waiting overnight risks muscle necrosis.

references.label: StatPearls. Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis treated with fasciotomy.

blueprintTopic: One normal pressure does not exclude compartment syndrome
vignette: A 24-year-old man has a crush injury of the forearm. Pain with passive finger extension is increasing. One intracompartmental pressure reading is 16 mm Hg. Delta pressure was not calculated. Blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg and pulse is 102/min. The forearm remains swollen.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge because one reading is under 30 mm Hg
Fasciotomy is forbidden after a normal reading
Start antibiotics and ignore the pressure
Apply a tight wrap to reduce the swelling
Admit him for serial examinations and pressures
correctAnswer: Admit him for serial examinations and pressures
explanation: A single pressure under 30 mm Hg does not exclude compartment syndrome. Pressures of 15 to 20 mm Hg in a high-risk limb are followed with serial measurements. A tight dressing would raise the pressure. "Discharge because one reading is under 30 mm Hg" is not the best choice because One normal value does not clear a worsening examination. "Fasciotomy is forbidden after a normal reading" is not the best choice because Fasciotomy is not forbidden. It is done if the exam or later pressures meet criteria. "Start antibiotics and ignore the pressure" is not the best choice because This presentation is ischemia from pressure, not a primary skin infection. "Apply a tight wrap to reduce the swelling" is not the best choice because External compression worsens compartment pressure.

references.label: StatPearls. Acute compartment syndrome. A single normal pressure does not exclude the diagnosis.

blueprintTopic: Naproxen for an acute gout flare
vignette: A 49-year-old man has 12 hours of a red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. He has had identical attacks that responded to anti-inflammatory drugs. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. He has no ulcer disease and no heart failure. Uric acid is 8.4 mg/dL. Temperature is 37.4 C and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: A three-month wait before any drug
Low-dose daily aspirin for the pain
Allopurinol alone starting tonight
Naproxen for the flare
Antibiotics without examining joint fluid
correctAnswer: Naproxen for the flare
explanation: An acute gout flare is treated with an anti-inflammatory drug started early. Naproxen is appropriate when kidneys, stomach, and heart are healthy. Allopurinol lowers urate over time and does not treat the flare by itself. "Allopurinol alone starting tonight" is not the best choice because Allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy. It does not replace an anti-inflammatory drug for the flare and can provoke flares. "Low-dose daily aspirin for the pain" is not the best choice because Low-dose aspirin is not used to treat gout pain and can raise urate. "Antibiotics without examining joint fluid" is not the best choice because A recurrent first-toe flare in a well patient is not automatically infection. "A three-month wait before any drug" is not the best choice because Treatment of a flare should start within the first day, not months later.

references.label: StatPearls. Gout. NSAIDs, colchicine, or glucocorticoids treat the flare. Allopurinol does not.

blueprintTopic: Avoid NSAIDs for gout when kidney function is low
vignette: A 70-year-old man has an acute first-toe gout flare. Creatinine clearance is 38 mL/min. He has no infection and no active ulcer. Uric acid is 9.1 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. He cannot take colchicine because of a prior severe reaction. Temperature is 37.2 C.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Allopurinol as the new drug
Low-dose aspirin around the clock
A short course of systemic glucocorticoid
Indomethacin because it is traditional for this patient
Full-dose naproxen for five days
correctAnswer: A short course of systemic glucocorticoid
