explanation: NSAIDs are avoided when creatinine clearance is under 60 mL/min. He also cannot take colchicine. A systemic glucocorticoid is an appropriate first-line treatment of the flare. "Full-dose naproxen for five days" is not the best choice because Naproxen is an NSAID and is contraindicated at this creatinine clearance. "Allopurinol as the new drug" is not the best choice because Allopurinol does not treat the inflammation of an acute flare. "Low-dose aspirin around the clock" is not the best choice because Aspirin is not recommended for gout flares. "Indomethacin because it is traditional for this patient" is not the best choice because Indomethacin is an NSAID with more toxicity and the same kidney contraindication.

references.label: StatPearls. Gout. NSAIDs are avoided when creatinine clearance is under 60 mL/min. Glucocorticoids are an alternative.

blueprintTopic: Do not use aspirin to treat a gout flare
vignette: A 55-year-old woman has a hot ankle and a serum uric acid of 7.6 mg/dL. Prior fluid showed needle-shaped crystals. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. She takes no anticoagulant. She asks to use the 81-mg aspirin in her cabinet for the pain. Temperature is 37.3 C and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Naproxen or colchicine for the flare
Probenecid as the acute pain drug
Start allopurinol and no anti-inflammatory drug
Vancomycin for presumed infection
Increase aspirin to treat the flare
correctAnswer: Naproxen or colchicine for the flare
explanation: Acute flares are treated with an NSAID, colchicine, or a glucocorticoid. Aspirin is not used for the flare. Low doses can raise serum urate. Her kidneys are normal, so naproxen is acceptable. "Increase aspirin to treat the flare" is not the best choice because Aspirin is not a treatment for gout pain and has paradoxical effects on urate. "Start allopurinol and no anti-inflammatory drug" is not the best choice because Urate-lowering therapy does not replace flare treatment. "Vancomycin for presumed infection" is not the best choice because Known crystal disease and a stable patient do not automatically need antibiotics. "Probenecid as the acute pain drug" is not the best choice because Probenecid is a uricosuric used for prevention, not for acute pain.

references.label: StatPearls. Gout. Aspirin is not recommended to treat flares.

blueprintTopic: Steroids for giant cell arteritis before biopsy
vignette: A 74-year-old woman has a new left-sided headache, jaw pain with chewing, and this morning a gray shade over the left eye that cleared. ESR is 78 mm/h. Temporal arteries are tender. Blood pressure is 150/86 mm Hg. Vision is 20/40 on the left. Biopsy has not been scheduled.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Temporal-artery biopsy before any steroid
High-dose glucocorticoids now
Observation because the vision cleared
Low-dose ibuprofen and a clinic visit next week
Anticoagulation for presumed retinal vein occlusion
correctAnswer: High-dose glucocorticoids now
explanation: New headache, jaw claudication, and transient vision loss after age 50 are giant cell arteritis until proved otherwise. High-dose glucocorticoids start immediately. Biopsy should not delay the first dose, especially when vision is threatened. "Temporal-artery biopsy before any steroid" is not the best choice because Waiting for a biopsy risks permanent vision loss. "Low-dose ibuprofen and a clinic visit next week" is not the best choice because An NSAID does not protect the optic nerve. "Observation because the vision cleared" is not the best choice because Amaurosis fugax is a warning, not a resolution. "Anticoagulation for presumed retinal vein occlusion" is not the best choice because This syndrome is arteritis, not a primary venous clot.

references.label: StatPearls. Giant cell arteritis. High-dose glucocorticoids are initial treatment and should not wait when vision is threatened.

blueprintTopic: Vision loss changes the steroid plan in arteritis
vignette: A 77-year-old man has had a temporal headache for five days. This afternoon the right eye went dark and has not recovered. The right pupil reacts poorly to light. ESR is 90 mm/h. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. He has not received steroids.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Schedule biopsy and start steroids next week
Oral prednisone 10 mg after biopsy returns
High-dose glucocorticoids immediately
Topical ophthalmic steroid drops
Aspirin alone for the headache
correctAnswer: High-dose glucocorticoids immediately
explanation: Established vision loss is a threatened-organ presentation of giant cell arteritis. High-dose systemic glucocorticoids are started at once. The route and dose are higher when vision is involved than for cranial symptoms alone, and drops do not treat arterial inflammation. "Oral prednisone 10 mg after biopsy returns" is not the best choice because A low dose after a delay does not treat ischemic optic neuropathy. "Aspirin alone for the headache" is not the best choice because Antiplatelet therapy is not the treatment of the arteritis. "Schedule biopsy and start steroids next week" is not the best choice because Vision loss cannot wait a week. "Topical ophthalmic steroid drops" is not the best choice because Drops do not reach the inflamed cranial artery.

references.label: StatPearls. Giant cell arteritis. Glucocorticoid dose and urgency depend on whether vision is threatened.

blueprintTopic: Operative debridement for necrotizing fasciitis
vignette: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has 10 hours of severe thigh pain after a minor skin nick. The skin is dusky, pain extends beyond the redness, and he is toxic. Temperature is 39.2 C, blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg, pulse 128/min, and lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. Glucose is 240 mg/dL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Intravenous antibiotics and a 24-hour check
Emergent operative exploration and debridement
CT scan and discharge if no abscess is seen
Oral antibiotics and warm compresses
Incision and drainage at the bedside tomorrow for this patient
correctAnswer: Emergent operative exploration and debridement
explanation: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, and shock are necrotizing fasciitis. Antibiotics are given, but the infection spreads along fascia and the next definitive step is emergent operative debridement. Imaging must not delay the operating room. "Intravenous antibiotics and a 24-hour check" is not the best choice because Antibiotics without surgery leave necrotic fascia in place. "Oral antibiotics and warm compresses" is not the best choice because This is septic shock, not cellulitis for home therapy. "Incision and drainage at the bedside tomorrow for this patient" is not the best choice because A delayed bedside nick is not a fasciotomy or a debridement. "CT scan and discharge if no abscess is seen" is not the best choice because Absence of a drainable abscess does not exclude fascial necrosis, and he is in shock.

references.label: StatPearls. Necrotizing fasciitis. Surgical debridement should not be delayed.

blueprintTopic: Fasciotomy when delta pressure is 30 mm Hg or less
vignette: A 33-year-old man has a tibial fracture and increasing calf pain. Diastolic blood pressure is 70 mm Hg. Intracompartmental pressure is 45 mm Hg. Pain increases when the toes are stretched. Pulse is 108/min and the foot is warm. He has received morphine without relief.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Elevation and a pressure check tomorrow in this case
Heparin for a presumed arterial clot
Discharge because the foot is warm
A nerve study scheduled next week
Fasciotomy for a delta pressure of 25 mm Hg
correctAnswer: Fasciotomy for a delta pressure of 25 mm Hg
explanation: Delta pressure is diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure, here 70 minus 45, which is 25 mm Hg. A delta pressure of 30 mm Hg or less is an indication for fasciotomy. A warm foot does not exclude muscle ischemia. "Discharge because the foot is warm" is not the best choice because pulses and warmth can persist after compartment pressure is already unsafe. "Elevation and a pressure check tomorrow in this case" is not the best choice because the delta pressure already meets the threshold for surgery. "Heparin for a presumed arterial clot" is not the best choice because the problem is pressure inside a closed compartment. "A nerve study scheduled next week" is not the best choice because electrodiagnostics do not decompress the compartment.

references.label: StatPearls. Acute compartment syndrome. Fasciotomy is indicated when delta pressure is 30 mm Hg or less.

blueprintTopic: Do not clear compartment syndrome by one soft reading
vignette: A 19-year-old man has a both-bone forearm fracture in a tight splint. He has increasing pain and numbness in the fingers. The splint is loosened. One pressure is 22 mm Hg. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse is 100/min. Pain with passive stretch persists.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Home with a sling because pressure is under 30 for this patient
A nerve-conduction study next week
Surgical consultation and monitored serial pressures
Therapeutic heparin overnight
Reapply a tighter splint for comfort
correctAnswer: Surgical consultation and monitored serial pressures
explanation: Pressures of 20 to 30 mm Hg with a persistent high-risk exam are admitted and shown to a surgeon. A value under 30 mm Hg is not clearance. Tightening the splint would raise compartment pressure. "Home with a sling because pressure is under 30 for this patient" is not the best choice because The number has not excluded the diagnosis, and the exam is worsening. "A nerve-conduction study next week" is not the best choice because Electrodiagnostics do not treat acute ischemia. "Therapeutic heparin overnight" is not the best choice because Anticoagulation does not open a tight osteofascial compartment. "Reapply a tighter splint for comfort" is not the best choice because External compression is harmful.

references.label: StatPearls. Compartment pressures of 20 to 30 mm Hg are admitted and the surgical team is consulted.

blueprintTopic: Ice is an adjunct, not the whole gout treatment
vignette: A 42-year-old man has 8 hours of podagra. He iced the toe. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, he has no heart failure, and he has no ulcer. Uric acid is 8.0 mg/dL. Temperature is 37.1 C and blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. He asks if ice is enough.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Prednisone for three months without a stop date
Ice alone for the next two weeks
Allopurinol tonight and stop the ice
Add an NSAID and continue rest and ice
Aspirin 81 mg four times a day
correctAnswer: Add an NSAID and continue rest and ice
explanation: Rest and ice help, and they are combined with an anti-inflammatory drug. An NSAID is appropriate with normal kidneys and no ulcer or heart failure. Ice alone does not replace that drug. "Ice alone for the next two weeks" is not the best choice because Non-drug measures are adjuncts. The flare needs an anti-inflammatory drug. "Allopurinol tonight and stop the ice" is not the best choice because Allopurinol is not acute flare therapy. "Aspirin 81 mg four times a day" is not the best choice because Aspirin is not used to treat the flare. "Prednisone for three months without a stop date" is not the best choice because Steroids treat a flare in a short course. Three months is not the plan when an NSAID is safe.

references.label: StatPearls. Gout flares are treated with an NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid, and ice may be added.

blueprintTopic: Native-joint cell count supports infection
vignette: A 60-year-old man has a native-knee effusion, fever of 38.7 C, and inability to bear weight. Synovial fluid has 72,000 white cells/uL with 94 percent neutrophils and no crystals. Gram stain is negative. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. Glucose is 160 mg/dL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Empiric intravenous antibiotics and drainage
Colchicine because fever can occur in gout
Send him home because the Gram stain is negative
Repeat the tap if fever lasts a week
Oral prednisone and no cultures
correctAnswer: Empiric intravenous antibiotics and drainage
explanation: A native-joint fluid white-cell count above 50,000 with neutrophil predominance suggests bacterial arthritis even when the Gram stain is negative. Antibiotics and drainage follow the aspiration. "Send him home because the Gram stain is negative" is not the best choice because Gram stain misses many infected joints. The cell count still indicates infection. "Colchicine because fever can occur in gout" is not the best choice because There are no crystals, and this cell count is treated as infection. "Repeat the tap if fever lasts a week" is not the best choice because Treatment is not delayed a week. "Oral prednisone and no cultures" is not the best choice because Steroids without antibiotics would worsen untreated infection.

references.label: StatPearls. Septic arthritis. Synovial fluid above 50,000 white cells with neutrophil predominance suggests bacteria.

blueprintTopic: Do not wait on the ESR to treat arteritis
vignette: A 71-year-old woman has jaw claudication and a new temporal headache. The laboratory has not reported the ESR because of a machine delay. She has had 20 minutes of monocular dimming. Blood pressure is 154/88 mm Hg and pulse is 84/min. The temporal artery is cord-like.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Carotid stenting for presumed atherosclerosis for this patient
Hold steroids until the ESR is in hand
Ibuprofen and a routine visit in ten days
Start high-dose glucocorticoids before the ESR returns
Temporal biopsy next month and no drug yet
correctAnswer: Start high-dose glucocorticoids before the ESR returns
explanation: The clinical syndrome plus transient visual loss is enough to start treatment. An ESR supports the diagnosis but its absence should not delay glucocorticoids when vision is at risk. "Hold steroids until the ESR is in hand" is not the best choice because A laboratory delay is not a reason to risk the eye. "Ibuprofen and a routine visit in ten days" is not the best choice because An NSAID does not treat arteritis. "Carotid stenting for presumed atherosclerosis for this patient" is not the best choice because Jaw claudication with a tender temporal artery is arteritis, not a stent lesion. "Temporal biopsy next month and no drug yet" is not the best choice because Biopsy can follow the first steroid dose. It should not be scheduled untreated for a month.

references.label: StatPearls. Giant cell arteritis. Start high-dose glucocorticoids when vision is threatened. Do not wait on confirmatory tests.

blueprintTopic: Loosen a splint that may be causing compartment pressure
vignette: A 30-year-old man has a distal radius fracture placed in a circumferential cast two hours ago. He now has increasing pain and tingling in the fingers. The cast is tight. Pain increases with passive finger motion. Blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg and pulse is 98/min. Capillary refill is 3 seconds.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation
Discharge with more oral opioid
Split the cast and reassess the compartments
Elevation alone and a visit next week for this patient
Add a second cast for more support
correctAnswer: Split the cast and reassess the compartments
explanation: A tight circumferential cast can cause compartment syndrome. It is split or removed immediately, and the limb is reexamined. If the exam remains diagnostic, fasciotomy follows. More casting and delayed follow-up are harmful. "Add a second cast for more support" is not the best choice because More constriction raises compartment pressure. "Discharge with more oral opioid" is not the best choice because Escalating pain and paresthesias are not treated with opioids and discharge. "Therapeutic anticoagulation" is not the best choice because The problem is external compression, not a new thrombus as the first issue. "Elevation alone and a visit next week for this patient" is not the best choice because Elevation does not remove a tight cast, and a week is too long.

references.label: StatPearls. Acute compartment syndrome. External compression is removed and the compartment is reassessed.

blueprintTopic: No transfusion at hemoglobin 8.4 when stable
vignette: A 54-year-old woman is hospitalized with pyelonephritis. She is afebrile after antibiotics, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, and pulse is 82/min. She has no coronary disease and no bleeding. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, unchanged from yesterday. She is walking in the hall.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Give plasma because the hemoglobin is low
Start erythropoietin tonight and transfuse now
No red-cell transfusion at this hemoglobin
Transfuse until hemoglobin exceeds 10 g/dL
Transfuse two units today
correctAnswer: No red-cell transfusion at this hemoglobin
explanation: A stable adult without coronary disease is transfused at a hemoglobin near 7 g/dL, not at 8.4 g/dL. She is walking and not bleeding. Observation and treatment of the infection are enough. "Transfuse two units today" is not the best choice because She is above the restrictive threshold and hemodynamically stable. "Transfuse until hemoglobin exceeds 10 g/dL" is not the best choice because A goal of 10 g/dL is not the restrictive strategy. "Give plasma because the hemoglobin is low" is not the best choice because Plasma does not treat anemia. "Start erythropoietin tonight and transfuse now" is not the best choice because Erythropoietin is not an emergency substitute, and transfusion is not indicated.

references.label: StatPearls. A restrictive transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL is appropriate for stable patients without acute coronary disease.

blueprintTopic: Observe mild asymptomatic thrombocytopenia
vignette: A 40-year-old man has a platelet count of 128,000/uL on a routine test. He has no bleeding, no new drug, and no fever. Hemoglobin is 14.6 g/dL and white cells are 6,200/uL. Blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. The smear shows no schistocytes. A count six months ago was 136,000/uL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Repeat the count and observe
Bone marrow biopsy this afternoon
Plasma exchange today
Platelet transfusion tonight
Start heparin for a low count
correctAnswer: Repeat the count and observe
explanation: Mild thrombocytopenia without bleeding or other cytopenias is rechecked and watched. Transfusion, plasma exchange, and marrow biopsy are for specific emergencies that are not present. "Platelet transfusion tonight" is not the best choice because He is not bleeding, and the count is far above any transfusion threshold. "Plasma exchange today" is not the best choice because Plasma exchange treats thrombotic microangiopathy, which he does not have. "Start heparin for a low count" is not the best choice because Heparin is not a treatment for thrombocytopenia and can cause it. "Bone marrow biopsy this afternoon" is not the best choice because Isolated mild thrombocytopenia does not need an emergency marrow examination.

references.label: StatPearls. Thrombocytopenia. Mild asymptomatic thrombocytopenia is monitored.

blueprintTopic: Transfuse earlier when coronary disease is present
vignette: A 73-year-old man with prior myocardial infarction and a coronary stent is admitted for pneumonia. He has no chest pain. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL. He is not bleeding. Oxygen saturation is 95 percent on 2 L.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Exchange transfusion for the anemia
Transfuse red cells using a threshold near 8 g/dL
Transfuse plasma instead of red cells
No transfusion because he has no chest pain
Withhold transfusion until hemoglobin is under 6 g/dL
correctAnswer: Transfuse red cells using a threshold near 8 g/dL
explanation: Patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease are managed with a higher restrictive threshold, about 8 g/dL, than the 7 g/dL threshold used for other stable adults. His hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL is below that threshold. "Withhold transfusion until hemoglobin is under 6 g/dL" is not the best choice because That cutoff is lower than the recommendation for coronary disease. "Transfuse plasma instead of red cells" is not the best choice because Plasma does not raise hemoglobin. "No transfusion because he has no chest pain" is not the best choice because The threshold does not require active ischemia. "Exchange transfusion for the anemia" is not the best choice because Exchange transfusion is not the treatment of ordinary anemia.

references.label: StatPearls. Use a hemoglobin threshold near 8 g/dL for patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease.

blueprintTopic: Low 4T score means HIT is unlikely
vignette: A 62-year-old man has been on heparin for three days after hip repair. Platelets fell from 240,000/uL to 190,000/uL. He has no thrombosis. The timing is early, the fall is small, and another cause is present. The 4T score is 2. Blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue heparin and look for other causes
Start bivalirudin because any fall is HIT for this patient
Transfuse platelets to above 200,000/uL
Start warfarin alone tonight
Stop heparin and start argatroban
correctAnswer: Continue heparin and look for other causes
explanation: A 4T score of 0 to 3 means heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is unlikely. Heparin may continue while another cause of the small platelet change is sought. Alternative anticoagulation is for a score of 4 or more. "Stop heparin and start argatroban" is not the best choice because That regimen is for intermediate or high probability, not a score of 2. "Start warfarin alone tonight" is not the best choice because Warfarin is not the treatment of a low-probability score, and it is dangerous in true HIT. "Transfuse platelets to above 200,000/uL" is not the best choice because He is not bleeding, and the count is nearly normal. "Start bivalirudin because any fall is HIT for this patient" is not the best choice because A small early fall is not treated as HIT.

references.label: StatPearls. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. A 4T score of 0 to 3 means HIT is unlikely.

blueprintTopic: Allopurinol before chemotherapy when uric acid is low
vignette: A 19-year-old man is about to start chemotherapy for a low-risk lymphoma that is not bulky. Uric acid is 6.2 mg/dL, potassium is 4.0 mEq/L, and creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. He has no G6PD deficiency. Urine output is good. The oncologist asks about prophylaxis for tumor lysis.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Rasburicase for each low-risk patient
Sodium bicarbonate in the intravenous fluid
Hydration and allopurinol
No fluids until chemotherapy ends
Calcium infusions during the first day
correctAnswer: Hydration and allopurinol
explanation: Before chemotherapy, when uric acid is under 8 mg/dL, allopurinol plus hydration is appropriate prophylaxis. Allopurinol blocks new uric acid formation. Rasburicase is preferred when risk is high or uric acid is already very high. "Rasburicase for each low-risk patient" is not the best choice because Rasburicase is for high-risk patients and established hyperuricemia, not for every low uric acid. "Sodium bicarbonate in the intravenous fluid" is not the best choice because Routine alkalinization is not recommended. It can worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation. "No fluids until chemotherapy ends" is not the best choice because Hydration should start before cells lyse. "Calcium infusions during the first day" is not the best choice because Prophylactic calcium is not part of prevention and can precipitate with phosphate.

references.label: StatPearls. Tumor lysis syndrome. Allopurinol is used for prevention when uric acid is under 8 mg/dL, with hydration.

blueprintTopic: Transfuse below 7 g/dL in a stable adult
vignette: A 48-year-old woman with a healed ankle fracture repair is on the ward. She has no heart disease and no bleeding. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse is 84/min. Hemoglobin is 6.5 g/dL. She is alert and the surgical site is dry.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Observe until hemoglobin is under 5 g/dL
Transfuse platelets for the anemia
Give iron intravenously and no red cells tonight
Transfuse red cells
Discharge without a blood count plan
correctAnswer: Transfuse red cells
explanation: For a stable hospitalized adult, the restrictive threshold is 7 g/dL. Her hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL is below that threshold, so red cells are indicated even though she is not in shock. "Observe until hemoglobin is under 5 g/dL" is not the best choice because The supported threshold is about 7 g/dL, not 5. "Transfuse platelets for the anemia" is not the best choice because Platelets do not correct a low hemoglobin. "Give iron intravenously and no red cells tonight" is not the best choice because Iron does not raise hemoglobin tonight in a patient already under the threshold. "Discharge without a blood count plan" is not the best choice because She needs transfusion, not an unplanned discharge.

references.label: StatPearls. Transfuse stable adults at a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL.

blueprintTopic: Heparin flushes still count in acute HIT
vignette: A 66-year-old woman has a central line flushed with heparin. Two days ago warfarin was started for a new calf-vein thrombus. She now has a painful necrotic patch on the thigh. Platelets fell from 260,000/uL to 55,000/uL. The 4T score is 6. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. She is not bleeding.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Switch the flushes to low-molecular-weight heparin in this case
Continue the flushes and increase warfarin
Ignore the skin and recheck platelets next week
Platelet transfusion and keep the heparin flushes
Stop heparin flushes, give vitamin K, and start argatroban
correctAnswer: Stop heparin flushes, give vitamin K, and start argatroban
explanation: Skin necrosis after warfarin is started during a platelet fall is acute heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Heparin flushes count as heparin and are stopped. Vitamin K reverses the warfarin, and a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban is started. "Continue the flushes and increase warfarin" is not the best choice because warfarin monotherapy in acute HIT risks further necrosis, and the flushes perpetuate the reaction. "Platelet transfusion and keep the heparin flushes" is not the best choice because she is not bleeding and heparin is the cause. "Switch the flushes to low-molecular-weight heparin in this case" is not the best choice because low-molecular-weight heparin can still drive HIT. "Ignore the skin and recheck platelets next week" is not the best choice because necrosis and a high 4T score are treated the same day.

references.label: StatPearls. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Stop all heparin, including flushes. Give vitamin K if warfarin was started, and use a non-heparin anticoagulant.

blueprintTopic: Delay warfarin until platelets recover from HIT
vignette: A 70-year-old man had definite HIT. Heparin was stopped and argatroban is therapeutic. Platelets have risen from 40,000/uL to 90,000/uL and are still climbing. He has no bleeding. INR from the argatroban effect is 2.4. Blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Transfuse platelets so warfarin can start
Treat the INR of 2.4 with vitamin K now
Stop argatroban and start warfarin tonight for this patient
Continue argatroban and do not start warfarin yet
Restart a heparin flush
correctAnswer: Continue argatroban and do not start warfarin yet
explanation: Warfarin starts only after the platelet count has substantially recovered, ideally to at least 150,000/uL, and it must overlap with therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulation. An argatroban-related INR is not a reason to stop the thrombin inhibitor. "Stop argatroban and start warfarin tonight for this patient" is not the best choice because Platelets have not recovered, and stopping the thrombin inhibitor leaves him unprotected. "Transfuse platelets so warfarin can start" is not the best choice because He is not bleeding. The count should recover on its own. "Restart a heparin flush" is not the best choice because Any heparin can relapse HIT while antibodies persist. "Treat the INR of 2.4 with vitamin K now" is not the best choice because Argatroban raises the INR without a vitamin K deficiency.

references.label: StatPearls. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Start warfarin only after platelets recover, overlapping a non-heparin anticoagulant.

blueprintTopic: Bleeding with drug-induced thrombocytopenia
vignette: A 52-year-old woman started a new antibiotic five days ago. She now has wet purpura and epistaxis. Platelets are 7,000/uL. Hemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL, creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, and coagulation times are normal. The smear shows no schistocytes. Temperature is 37.0 C and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop the new drug and transfuse platelets
Plasma exchange for presumed microangiopathy
Heparin infusion for the low platelet count
Observation because coagulation times are normal
Vitamin K as the hemostatic drug
correctAnswer: Stop the new drug and transfuse platelets
explanation: She is bleeding with severe thrombocytopenia, a new drug, a normal smear, and normal coagulation studies. Stop the drug. Platelet transfusion is appropriate when severe thrombocytopenia is accompanied by bleeding. This is not thrombotic microangiopathy. "Plasma exchange for presumed microangiopathy" is not the best choice because there are no schistocytes, no renal injury, and no fever to suggest that diagnosis. "Heparin infusion for the low platelet count" is not the best choice because heparin does not treat thrombocytopenia and can cause it. "Observation because coagulation times are normal" is not the best choice because she is actively bleeding with a platelet count of 7,000/uL. "Vitamin K as the hemostatic drug" is not the best choice because coagulation times are normal, so this is not a vitamin K deficiency.

references.label: StatPearls. Thrombocytopenia. Bleeding with severe thrombocytopenia is treated with platelet transfusion, and the offending drug is stopped.

blueprintTopic: Do not give rasburicase in G6PD deficiency
vignette: A 16-year-old boy with known G6PD deficiency has Burkitt lymphoma. After chemotherapy, uric acid is 14 mg/dL, potassium is 5.6 mEq/L, and creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. He has no tetany. Blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Urine output is present.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Hydration plus febuxostat, not rasburicase
Rasburicase as the uric-acid drug
Calcium infusion for prevention
Sodium bicarbonate in the fluids
No uric-acid drug and fluid restriction today
correctAnswer: Hydration plus febuxostat, not rasburicase
explanation: Rasburicase produces hydrogen peroxide and can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, so it is contraindicated here. Febuxostat can be used when rasburicase is contraindicated, together with potassium-free hydration. "Rasburicase as the uric-acid drug" is not the best choice because of the G6PD deficiency. "Calcium infusion for prevention" is not the best choice because he has no symptomatic hypocalcemia. "Sodium bicarbonate in the fluids" is not the best choice because routine alkalinization is avoided. "No uric-acid drug and fluid restriction today" is not the best choice because established tumor lysis needs volume and a uric-acid strategy he can safely receive.

references.label: StatPearls. Tumor lysis syndrome. Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency. Febuxostat is an alternative when rasburicase cannot be used.

blueprintTopic: Do not alkalinize urine routinely in tumor lysis
vignette: A 12-year-old girl is starting therapy for high-risk leukemia. Uric acid is 5.5 mg/dL, potassium is 4.1 mEq/L, and phosphate is 4.0 mg/dL. Creatinine is 0.5 mg/dL. Rasburicase is available. A resident asks to add bicarbonate to the intravenous fluids. She has no metabolic acidosis.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Give calcium with the bicarbonate
Add bicarbonate to the intravenous fluid
Hydration without routine bicarbonate
Hold fluids until the uric acid rises
Use bicarbonate and skip a uric-acid drug
correctAnswer: Hydration without routine bicarbonate
explanation: Routine urinary alkalinization is not recommended. Bicarbonate can lower ionized calcium and promote calcium-phosphate precipitation. It is considered only for metabolic acidosis when rasburicase is unavailable. She has neither indication. "Add bicarbonate to the intravenous fluid" is not the best choice because That is the practice the guidance warns against. "Hold fluids until the uric acid rises" is not the best choice because Hydration is the core of prevention and should not be withheld. "Give calcium with the bicarbonate" is not the best choice because Prophylactic calcium is not indicated. "Use bicarbonate and skip a uric-acid drug" is not the best choice because She may need allopurinol or rasburicase based on risk. Bicarbonate is not a substitute.

references.label: StatPearls. Tumor lysis syndrome. Routine bicarbonate is avoided. Use it only for acidosis when rasburicase is unavailable.

blueprintTopic: Antibiotics within the hour for febrile neutropenia
vignette: A 58-year-old man with leukemia has a temperature of 38.6 C. Absolute neutrophil count is 180/uL. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. He looks ill. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Cultures have been drawn. No antibiotic has been given. The expected neutropenia will last more than seven days.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Vancomycin alone with no gram-negative drug
Oral amoxicillin and discharge
Wait for the culture result tonight
Intravenous antipseudomonal monotherapy now
Acetaminophen and a clinic visit tomorrow
correctAnswer: Intravenous antipseudomonal monotherapy now
explanation: High-risk febrile neutropenia is treated with an intravenous antipseudomonal beta-lactam, such as cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam, within an hour after cultures. Treatment does not wait on culture results. "Wait for the culture result tonight" is not the best choice because Bacteremia can progress during the wait. Antibiotics start empirically. "Oral amoxicillin and discharge" is not the best choice because He is high risk because neutropenia will be prolonged. Oral therapy and discharge are not the plan. "Vancomycin alone with no gram-negative drug" is not the best choice because Monotherapy must cover Pseudomonas. Vancomycin alone does not. "Acetaminophen and a clinic visit tomorrow" is not the best choice because Fever during profound neutropenia is an emergency.

references.label: StatPearls. Febrile neutropenia. High-risk patients receive an intravenous antipseudomonal beta-lactam within one hour.

blueprintTopic: ATRA plus arsenic for low-risk promyelocytic leukemia
vignette: A 44-year-old man has confirmed PML-RARA acute promyelocytic leukemia. White cells are 3,200/uL and platelets are 88,000/uL. He has no heart failure. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL. INR is 1.3. Blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. Induction has not started.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Hydroxyurea as the induction drug
Observation until the white count exceeds 20,000/uL
Delay therapy until after a six-week vacation
Cytarabine and daunorubicin without a differentiating agent
All-trans retinoic acid plus arsenic trioxide
correctAnswer: All-trans retinoic acid plus arsenic trioxide
explanation: White cells of 10,000/uL or less and platelets of 40,000/uL or more define low-risk acute promyelocytic leukemia. All-trans retinoic acid plus arsenic trioxide is the induction standard for low-risk disease and is less toxic than anthracycline-based chemotherapy. "Cytarabine and daunorubicin without a differentiating agent" is not the best choice because ordinary AML induction omits the differentiating therapy this leukemia requires. "Observation until the white count exceeds 20,000/uL" is not the best choice because treatment is not delayed to watch the count rise. "Hydroxyurea as the induction drug" is not the best choice because cytoreduction does not replace differentiating therapy. "Delay therapy until after a six-week vacation" is not the best choice because this leukemia is treated promptly even when the count is low.

references.label: StatPearls. Acute promyelocytic leukemia. ATRA plus arsenic trioxide is standard induction for low-risk disease.

blueprintTopic: No prophylactic plasma for a mild INR
vignette: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis needs a paracentesis. INR is 1.6 and platelets are 90,000/uL. He is not bleeding. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL. A resident orders four units of plasma to correct the INR before the tap.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Give factor VIIa before the procedure
Transfuse platelets to above 150,000/uL first for this patient
Perform the paracentesis without prophylactic plasma
Cancel the tap because the INR is 1.6
Transfuse plasma until the INR is 1.0
correctAnswer: Perform the paracentesis without prophylactic plasma
explanation: In liver disease, INR does not predict procedural bleeding. Prophylactic plasma is not indicated for a low-bleeding-risk procedure such as paracentesis in a patient who is not bleeding, especially when the INR is between 1.5 and 1.9. "Transfuse plasma until the INR is 1.0" is not the best choice because Plasma will not reliably normalize the INR and is not recommended. "Give factor VIIa before the procedure" is not the best choice because Factor VIIa is not routine prophylaxis for paracentesis. "Cancel the tap because the INR is 1.6" is not the best choice because The tap is the indicated procedure. The INR is not a reason to cancel it. "Transfuse platelets to above 150,000/uL first for this patient" is not the best choice because A count of 90,000/uL does not require transfusion before paracentesis.

references.label: StatPearls. Prophylactic plasma is not supported before low-risk procedures when the patient is not bleeding.

blueprintTopic: Do not give calcium for asymptomatic tumor-lysis hypocalcemia
vignette: A 14-year-old boy with tumor lysis has phosphate of 8.0 mg/dL and calcium of 6.8 mg/dL. He has no tetany, no seizures, and a normal ECG. Potassium is 5.2 mEq/L and creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. He is receiving hydration. Blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Sodium bicarbonate to chase the calcium up for this patient
Phosphate binding and hydration without calcium
Stop hydration because calcium is low
Observation with no phosphate plan
Intravenous calcium for the number alone
correctAnswer: Phosphate binding and hydration without calcium
explanation: Hypocalcemia in tumor lysis is driven by high phosphate. Calcium given to an asymptomatic patient precipitates with phosphate and can worsen kidney injury. Treat the phosphate and keep hydrating. Give calcium only for symptoms or ECG changes. "Intravenous calcium for the number alone" is not the best choice because The number without symptoms is not treated with calcium in this setting. "Stop hydration because calcium is low" is not the best choice because Hydration is still required. "Sodium bicarbonate to chase the calcium up for this patient" is not the best choice because Alkalinization can further lower ionized calcium. "Observation with no phosphate plan" is not the best choice because Phosphate of 8 mg/dL needs a binder and volume, not observation alone.

references.label: StatPearls. Tumor lysis syndrome. Do not give calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcemia caused by hyperphosphatemia.

blueprintTopic: Exudate by pleural protein ratio
vignette: A 67-year-old man has a right pleural effusion. Pleural fluid protein is 4.6 g/dL and serum protein is 6.8 g/dL. He has fever of 38.4 C and a cough. Blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg and pulse is 96/min. Lactate dehydrogenase results are still pending.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge without thoracentesis results
No further tests because one value is pending for this patient
Treat and investigate this fluid as an exudate
Label it a transudate and give a diuretic
Start dialysis for the protein ratio
correctAnswer: Treat and investigate this fluid as an exudate
explanation: Light criteria call the fluid an exudate if the pleural-to-serum protein ratio is above 0.5. Here the ratio is about 0.68. One met criterion is enough. Infection is investigated rather than treating the fluid as heart-failure fluid. "Label it a transudate and give a diuretic" is not the best choice because The protein ratio already classifies an exudate. "No further tests because one value is pending for this patient" is not the best choice because The protein ratio does not require the LDH result. "Start dialysis for the protein ratio" is not the best choice because The ratio is a classification tool, not a dialysis indication. "Discharge without thoracentesis results" is not the best choice because An exudate needs a cause, especially with fever.

references.label: StatPearls. Pleural effusion. Protein ratio above 0.5 meets Light criteria for an exudate.

blueprintTopic: Heart-failure fluid is managed as a transudate
vignette: A 74-year-old man with known heart failure has dyspnea. Pleural fluid protein is 1.8 g/dL and serum protein is 6.6 g/dL. He has no fever. Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, pulse is 98/min, and oxygen saturation is 93 percent. The effusion is moderate and he is comfortable on 2 L of oxygen.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Diuresis and treat the heart failure
Empiric antibiotics for seven days
Pleurodesis tomorrow morning
Thoracotomy for a trapped lung
A chest tube as the first treatment for this patient
correctAnswer: Diuresis and treat the heart failure
explanation: The protein ratio is about 0.27, so no Light criterion given here is met and the fluid is a transudate. Heart failure is treated. A chest tube is not first-line for a moderate, tolerated transudate. "A chest tube as the first treatment for this patient" is not the best choice because Drainage is for symptom relief that medicines do not provide, not the first step here. "Empiric antibiotics for seven days" is not the best choice because He has no fever or other sign that this is an empyema. "Pleurodesis tomorrow morning" is not the best choice because Pleurodesis is for recurrent malignant or refractory effusions. "Thoracotomy for a trapped lung" is not the best choice because Nothing suggests a trapped lung.

references.label: StatPearls. Pleural effusion. Heart failure causes a transudate. If no Light criterion is met, the fluid is transudative.

blueprintTopic: Albumin gradient when heart failure looks exudative
vignette: A 78-year-old man on diuretics for heart failure has a pleural effusion. Pleural protein is 3.4 g/dL and serum protein is 6.2 g/dL. Serum albumin is 3.6 g/dL and pleural albumin is 2.1 g/dL. He has no fever, no weight loss, and a known low ejection fraction. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Diagnose tuberculosis from these numbers
Treat heart failure; the albumin gradient fits a transudate
Pleurodesis before any diuretic change
Place a chest tube and start antibiotics for this patient today
Start a cancer workup as the plan
correctAnswer: Treat heart failure; the albumin gradient fits a transudate
explanation: Diuretics can push a heart-failure effusion across a Light protein cutoff. The serum-to-fluid albumin gradient is 1.5 g/dL, above 1.2 g/dL, which supports a transudate. Heart failure is treated rather than labeling the fluid malignant. "Start a cancer workup as the plan" is not the best choice because The gradient explains a pseudoexudate. Cancer is not the first conclusion. "Place a chest tube and start antibiotics for this patient today" is not the best choice because There is no evidence of infection. "Diagnose tuberculosis from these numbers" is not the best choice because Protein numbers do not diagnose tuberculosis. "Pleurodesis before any diuretic change" is not the best choice because Optimize heart-failure treatment before pleurodesis.

references.label: StatPearls. Pleural effusion. In heart failure, an albumin gradient above 1.2 g/dL supports a transudate when Light criteria misclassify the fluid.

blueprintTopic: Hemothorax when the fluid hematocrit is half the blood
vignette: A 36-year-old man has chest pain after a fall. The pleural fluid is bloody. Fluid hematocrit is 24 percent and blood hematocrit is 40 percent. Blood pressure is 100/64 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min. Oxygen saturation is 94 percent. Breath sounds are reduced on the left.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Anticoagulate for a pulmonary embolus
Observe because the fluid is blood-tinged
Give diuretics for a transudate
Drain the hemothorax with a chest tube
Start antibiotics and no drainage
correctAnswer: Drain the hemothorax with a chest tube
explanation: Hemothorax is present when the pleural-fluid hematocrit is more than half the blood hematocrit. Twenty-four percent is more than half of 40 percent. A traumatic hemothorax is drained. "Observe because the fluid is blood-tinged" is not the best choice because The hematocrit ratio defines a hemothorax, not a trivial stain. "Start antibiotics and no drainage" is not the best choice because Blood in the pleura is not treated with antibiotics alone. "Give diuretics for a transudate" is not the best choice because This ratio is blood, not a transudate. "Anticoagulate for a pulmonary embolus" is not the best choice because Anticoagulation would worsen traumatic bleeding.

references.label: StatPearls. Pleural effusion. Hemothorax is a fluid hematocrit more than half the blood hematocrit.

blueprintTopic: Chylothorax when triglycerides are high
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has a milky pleural effusion after neck surgery. Pleural triglycerides are 180 mg/dL. She is afebrile. Blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. The fluid is sterile on Gram stain.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start four-drug tuberculosis therapy
Treat it as empyema with fibrinolytics
Manage this as a chylothorax
Label it a transudate and give a diuretic
Anticoagulate for hemothorax
correctAnswer: Manage this as a chylothorax
explanation: Pleural triglycerides above 110 mg/dL in milky fluid diagnose chylothorax. Management addresses the leak, often with drainage and dietary fat modification or a procedure, not antibiotics for pus she does not have. "Treat it as empyema with fibrinolytics" is not the best choice because The fluid is sterile and milky, not pus. "Start four-drug tuberculosis therapy" is not the best choice because Triglycerides do not diagnose tuberculosis. "Label it a transudate and give a diuretic" is not the best choice because Chyle is not a heart-failure transudate. "Anticoagulate for hemothorax" is not the best choice because The fluid is chyle, not blood.

references.label: StatPearls. Pleural effusion. Triglycerides above 110 mg/dL indicate chylothorax.

blueprintTopic: Lung cancer screening when criteria are met
vignette: A 62-year-old man has smoked one pack daily for 30 years and still smokes. He has no symptoms. He quit nothing. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. He asks whether any imaging is recommended to look for lung cancer.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: PET-CT as the screening test
Chest radiograph each year
No imaging until he has a cough for this patient
Sputum cytology twice a year
Annual low-dose CT while he remains eligible
correctAnswer: Annual low-dose CT while he remains eligible
explanation: USPSTF recommends annual low-dose CT for adults 50 to 80 years old with at least a 20 pack-year history who smoke or quit within the past 15 years. A chest radiograph is not the screening test. "Chest radiograph each year" is not the best choice because Radiographs are not the recommended screening modality. "No imaging until he has a cough for this patient" is not the best choice because Screening is for asymptomatic people who meet criteria. "Sputum cytology twice a year" is not the best choice because Cytology is not the screening test. "PET-CT as the screening test" is not the best choice because PET is not used to screen an asymptomatic person.

references.label: USPSTF. Annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in eligible adults with a substantial smoking history.

blueprintTopic: Do not screen for lung cancer outside the age range
vignette: A 42-year-old man has smoked a pack daily for 8 years. He has no symptoms, no asbestos exposure, and no personal cancer history. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. He requests a screening CT because a coworker had lung cancer.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Order a PET-CT this month
Counsel that screening CT is not indicated
Order annual low-dose CT
Start a chest radiograph series
Obtain sputum cytology twice a year for this patient
correctAnswer: Counsel that screening CT is not indicated
explanation: He is under 50 and has about 8 pack-years. USPSTF screening starts at age 50 with at least 20 pack-years. A screening CT would be more likely to harm than to help. "Order annual low-dose CT" is not the best choice because He does not meet age or pack-year criteria. "Order a PET-CT this month" is not the best choice because PET is not a screening test. "Start a chest radiograph series" is not the best choice because Radiographs are not recommended screening. "Obtain sputum cytology twice a year for this patient" is not the best choice because Cytology is not recommended screening.

references.label: USPSTF. Lung cancer screening is for ages 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years.

blueprintTopic: Fluid restriction for mildly symptomatic SIADH
vignette: A 68-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer has sodium of 128 mEq/L. He is alert and has no seizures. Serum osmolality is 262 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 520 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium is 45 mEq/L. He is euvolemic. TSH and cortisol are normal. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Normal saline and a loop diuretic immediately
Bolus 3 percent saline now
Demeclocycline as the first drug tonight
Isotonic saline at 200 mL per hour
Restrict free water intake
correctAnswer: Restrict free water intake
explanation: This is SIADH: hypo-osmolar hyponatremia, inappropriately concentrated urine, and euvolemia, with thyroid and adrenal disease excluded. Mild symptoms are treated with free-water restriction, generally under about 800 mL per day. Hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms. "Bolus 3 percent saline now" is not the best choice because He has no seizures, deep confusion, or other severe symptoms. "Isotonic saline at 200 mL per hour" is not the best choice because Isotonic saline can worsen SIADH when urine is more concentrated than the infusate. "Demeclocycline as the first drug tonight" is not the best choice because Drugs are not first-line for mild SIADH. "Normal saline and a loop diuretic immediately" is not the best choice because That combination is not the initial step for mild symptoms.

references.label: StatPearls. SIADH. Mild symptoms are treated with fluid restriction. Isotonic saline may worsen the sodium.

blueprintTopic: Hypertonic saline for severely symptomatic SIADH
vignette: A 60-year-old woman with SIADH has a seizure. Sodium is 114 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 242 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality is 610 mOsm/kg. She is euvolemic. Blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. You plan the first change in the sodium.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Normal saline and no sodium checks
Isotonic saline wide open
Correct the sodium by 20 mEq in the next six hours for this patient
Fluid restriction alone during the seizure
3 percent saline with a limit near 8 mEq in 24 hours
correctAnswer: 3 percent saline with a limit near 8 mEq in 24 hours
explanation: A seizure is severe symptoms. Hypertonic saline is used because urine osmolality is high and isotonic saline will not reliably raise the sodium. The rise should not exceed about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination. "Isotonic saline wide open" is not the best choice because Isotonic saline can lower the sodium further when urine is very concentrated. "Fluid restriction alone during the seizure" is not the best choice because Restriction is too slow for active seizures. "Normal saline and no sodium checks" is not the best choice because Unchecked correction is how demyelination occurs. "Correct the sodium by 20 mEq in the next six hours for this patient" is not the best choice because That rate is far above the safe limit.

references.label: StatPearls. SIADH. Severe symptoms are treated with 3 percent saline. Do not exceed about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.

blueprintTopic: Isotonic saline for rhabdomyolysis
vignette: A 27-year-old man is found on the floor after a long lie. Creatine kinase is 48,000 U/L. Potassium is 5.1 mEq/L and creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. He is awake. Blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. Urine is tea-colored and output is low.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Hemodialysis as the first step
Restrict fluids to prevent swelling
Furosemide before any fluid
Sodium bicarbonate in the fluid bags
Large-volume isotonic saline
correctAnswer: Large-volume isotonic saline
explanation: The immediate goal in rhabdomyolysis is volume resuscitation to maintain urine output and limit kidney injury. Isotonic saline is started promptly. Dialysis is for complications such as refractory hyperkalemia or overload, not the first step in a patient who can take fluid. "Furosemide before any fluid" is not the best choice because A diuretic in a volume-depleted patient worsens kidney injury. "Sodium bicarbonate in the fluid bags" is not the best choice because Bicarbonate is not required initial therapy. "Hemodialysis as the first step" is not the best choice because He has no refractory indication for dialysis yet. "Restrict fluids to prevent swelling" is not the best choice because Restriction is the opposite of the needed resuscitation.

references.label: StatPearls. Rhabdomyolysis. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is the core of early management.

blueprintTopic: Saline first for symptomatic hypercalcemia
vignette: A 69-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer has calcium of 13.6 mg/dL. He is confused and polyuric. Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min. Creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. He has dry mucous membranes. PTH is suppressed.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Isotonic saline until he is euvolemic
Furosemide as the first drug
Zoledronic acid before any fluid
Calcitonin as the treatment
Restrict fluids because of the cancer
correctAnswer: Isotonic saline until he is euvolemic
explanation: Severe hypercalcemia causes volume depletion. Isotonic saline is the first treatment and restores glomerular filtration. A bisphosphonate is added for malignancy, but it works over days and does not replace initial volume. "Zoledronic acid before any fluid" is not the best choice because The bisphosphonate is appropriate later. It is not a substitute for resuscitation of a hypotensive patient. "Furosemide as the first drug" is not the best choice because Loop diuretics are used only after volume is restored, if at all. "Calcitonin as the treatment" is not the best choice because Calcitonin can bridge a few hours. It does not replace saline. "Restrict fluids because of the cancer" is not the best choice because He is dry. Restriction worsens hypercalcemia.

references.label: StatPearls. Hypercalcemia. Volume resuscitation with isotonic saline is the first step.

blueprintTopic: Dialysis when hypercalcemia meets kidney failure
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with myeloma has calcium of 15.2 mg/dL. She is anuric for 12 hours, has pulmonary edema, and cannot tolerate more intravenous fluid. Creatinine is 5.4 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 160/96 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 90 percent. PTH is low.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: A thiazide to reduce urine calcium
Oral phosphorus binders as the step
Observation overnight
Renal replacement therapy with a low-calcium bath
More isotonic saline despite pulmonary edema for this patient
correctAnswer: Renal replacement therapy with a low-calcium bath
explanation: Dialysis is reserved for severe hypercalcemia with kidney failure or for patients who cannot tolerate intravenous volume. She is anuric and fluid-overloaded, so more saline is unsafe. A low- or no-calcium bath removes calcium. "More isotonic saline despite pulmonary edema for this patient" is not the best choice because Additional saline will worsen oxygenation. "Observation overnight" is not the best choice because Calcium of 15 mg/dL with anuria is not observed. "Oral phosphorus binders as the step" is not the best choice because Binders do not treat this emergency. "A thiazide to reduce urine calcium" is not the best choice because Thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and can worsen hypercalcemia. She is anuric anyway.

references.label: StatPearls. Hypercalcemia. Dialysis is for severe hypercalcemia with kidney failure or inability to tolerate saline.

blueprintTopic: Intubate ongoing hematemesis when the airway is unprotected
vignette: A 64-year-old man is vomiting large amounts of blood and cannot clear his airway. He opens his eyes only to pain and groans. Blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg and pulse is 128/min. Oxygen saturation is 90 percent on a nonrebreather mask. One large-bore intravenous line is running.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Oral omeprazole and a ride home
A barium swallow before any other step
Nasogastric lavage as the airway plan in this case
Observation until the vomiting stops
Endotracheal intubation for airway protection
correctAnswer: Endotracheal intubation for airway protection
explanation: Ongoing severe hematemesis with a depressed mental status means he cannot protect his airway. Endotracheal intubation is indicated while resuscitation continues. A barium study and discharge are not safe. "Oral omeprazole and a ride home" is not the best choice because he is in shock and cannot protect his airway. "A barium swallow before any other step" is not the best choice because contrast will obscure later endoscopy and does not secure the airway. "Observation until the vomiting stops" is not the best choice because he is already hypoxic and poorly responsive. "Nasogastric lavage as the airway plan in this case" is not the best choice because a lavage tube does not protect the airway from massive hematemesis.

references.label: StatPearls. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Intubate when the patient cannot protect the airway or has ongoing severe hematemesis.

blueprintTopic: Resuscitate unstable upper gastrointestinal bleeding
vignette: A 58-year-old man vomits blood. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg and pulse is 130/min. Hemoglobin is 7.1 g/dL. He has one 22-gauge intravenous line. He is drowsy. Oxygen saturation is 94 percent on room air.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Two large-bore intravenous lines and rapid resuscitation
Oral sucralfate and a clinic visit
Discharge with a proton-pump inhibitor
Schedule endoscopy for next week
Observation with no fluids until endoscopy for this patient
correctAnswer: Two large-bore intravenous lines and rapid resuscitation
explanation: Unstable upper gastrointestinal bleeding is resuscitated first. At least two large-bore intravenous lines and volume, including blood as needed, come before a delayed endoscopy. Early resuscitation lowers mortality. "Discharge with a proton-pump inhibitor" is not the best choice because Shock and hematemesis are not an outpatient problem. "Schedule endoscopy for next week" is not the best choice because Endoscopy is urgent after resuscitation, not next week. "Oral sucralfate and a clinic visit" is not the best choice because A coating agent does not treat hemorrhagic shock. "Observation with no fluids until endoscopy for this patient" is not the best choice because He needs volume now. Endoscopy is unsafe without resuscitation.

references.label: StatPearls. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Resuscitate with large-bore access before endoscopy.

blueprintTopic: Cefotaxime when ascitic neutrophils exceed 250
vignette: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis has new abdominal pain and fever of 38.3 C. Ascitic fluid has 480 neutrophils/uL. Gram stain shows no organisms. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL and bilirubin is 1.4 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg and pulse is 100/min.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Large-volume paracentesis as the treatment
Wait for the culture before any antibiotic
Oral metronidazole alone
Albumin and no antibiotic because creatinine is normal
Intravenous cefotaxime
correctAnswer: Intravenous cefotaxime
explanation: Ascitic neutrophils above 250/uL with a compatible illness are spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. A third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime is started empirically. Culture results are not required first. His creatinine and bilirubin do not meet the usual albumin thresholds. "Wait for the culture before any antibiotic" is not the best choice because Cultures are often negative. Treatment starts at the cell-count threshold. "Oral metronidazole alone" is not the best choice because Metronidazole does not cover the typical gram-negative organisms. "Large-volume paracentesis as the treatment" is not the best choice because Removing fluid does not treat the infection. "Albumin and no antibiotic because creatinine is normal" is not the best choice because Albumin is adjunctive when kidney or bilirubin criteria are met. Antibiotics are still required.

references.label: StatPearls. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Start a third-generation cephalosporin when neutrophils exceed 250/uL.

blueprintTopic: Albumin for SBP when creatinine is high
vignette: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis has ascitic neutrophils of 600/uL and fever of 38.1 C. Cefotaxime has just been ordered. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, BUN is 34 mg/dL, and bilirubin is 2.0 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Give octreotide instead of albumin
No adjunct because bilirubin is under 4 mg/dL
Stop the antibiotic and give albumin
Add albumin if creatinine exceeds 3 mg/dL
Add intravenous albumin to the antibiotic
correctAnswer: Add intravenous albumin to the antibiotic
explanation: Albumin is added to antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis when creatinine is above 1 mg/dL, BUN is above 30 mg/dL, or bilirubin is above 4 mg/dL. She meets the creatinine and BUN criteria. Albumin lowers the risk of kidney injury. "Stop the antibiotic and give albumin" is not the best choice because Albumin is adjunctive. The antibiotic stays. "Add albumin if creatinine exceeds 3 mg/dL" is not the best choice because The threshold used here is about 1 mg/dL, which she has passed. "Give octreotide instead of albumin" is not the best choice because Octreotide is not the substitute for this albumin indication. "No adjunct because bilirubin is under 4 mg/dL" is not the best choice because Any one of the three criteria is enough. Creatinine already qualifies.

references.label: StatPearls. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Give albumin when creatinine, BUN, or bilirubin thresholds are met.

blueprintTopic: Lactulose first for hepatic encephalopathy
vignette: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis is confused. Asterixis is present. Ammonia is 90 umol/L. He has not received lactulose. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and he has no gastrointestinal bleeding. A family member asks for rifaximin first.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start rifaximin and skip lactulose
No treatment because some patients have a normal ammonia
Restrict dietary protein permanently
Give benzodiazepines for the agitation
Start lactulose and look for a precipitant
correctAnswer: Start lactulose and look for a precipitant
explanation: Once hepatic encephalopathy is clinically present, lactulose is first-line ammonia-lowering therapy, whether or not the ammonia number is high. A precipitant such as infection, bleeding, or a sedative is sought. Rifaximin is added when lactulose fails or is not tolerated. "Start rifaximin and skip lactulose" is not the best choice because Rifaximin is second-line, not a replacement for the first drug. "Restrict dietary protein permanently" is not the best choice because Nutrition is supported. Long-term protein restriction is harmful. "Give benzodiazepines for the agitation" is not the best choice because Sedatives can precipitate encephalopathy. "No treatment because some patients have a normal ammonia" is not the best choice because The decision follows the clinical diagnosis, not a normal or high ammonia alone.

references.label: StatPearls. Hepatic encephalopathy. Lactulose is first-line. Rifaximin is for patients who do not respond.

blueprintTopic: Very low Glasgow-Blatchford score may go home
vignette: A 32-year-old man had one episode of coffee-ground emesis that has stopped. Hemoglobin is 14.8 g/dL. Systolic blood pressure is 128 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. He has no melena, syncope, heart failure, or liver disease. He is hungry and walking. Urea is normal. The Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge with close outpatient follow-up
Start octreotide and a beta blocker
Intubate for airway protection
Transfuse one unit before discharge for this patient
Admit for urgent endoscopy tonight
correctAnswer: Discharge with close outpatient follow-up
explanation: A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 or 1 identifies patients who can be discharged with outpatient follow-up. He has none of the score's risk features. Urgent admission and endoscopy are for higher scores. "Admit for urgent endoscopy tonight" is not the best choice because The score was built to avoid that admission when it is 0. "Transfuse one unit before discharge for this patient" is not the best choice because Hemoglobin is normal. "Start octreotide and a beta blocker" is not the best choice because Those drugs are for variceal bleeding, which he has no evidence of. "Intubate for airway protection" is not the best choice because He is protecting his airway and the bleeding has stopped.

references.label: StatPearls. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding. A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 or 1 can be managed with outpatient follow-up.

blueprintTopic: Number needed to treat from absolute risk reduction
vignette: A randomized trial of a new anticoagulant enrolls adults with atrial fibrillation. Over one year, stroke occurs in 8 of 100 patients on the new drug and in 18 of 100 patients on the comparator. No one is lost. You are asked for the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke in a year.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: About 26 patients treated for one year
The number cannot be calculated from these counts
About 2 patients treated for one year
About 10 patients treated for one year
About 50 patients treated for one year
correctAnswer: About 10 patients treated for one year
explanation: Absolute risk reduction is 0.18 minus 0.08, which is 0.10. Number needed to treat is 1 divided by 0.10, which is 10. About 10 patients must be treated for one year to prevent one stroke. "About 2 patients treated for one year" is not the best choice because That figure treats the relative reduction, 10 percentage points over 18, as if it were the absolute denominator. "About 26 patients treated for one year" is not the best choice because That is not 1 divided by the absolute difference of 0.10. "About 50 patients treated for one year" is not the best choice because Fifty would match an absolute reduction of 2 percentage points, not 10. "The number cannot be calculated from these counts" is not the best choice because Both event rates are given, so the number can be calculated.

references.label: Irwig et al. Smart Health Choices. Number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction. NCBI Bookshelf NBK63647.

blueprintTopic: A confidence interval that includes 1
vignette: A randomized trial reports an absolute risk reduction of 10 percent for a new drug. The 95 percent confidence interval for that reduction runs from -5 percent to 25 percent. The authors write that the drug works because the point estimate is above zero.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The negative bound proves the drug is harmful
The interval includes zero, so the difference is not significant
The point estimate proves a clear 10 percent benefit
The result is significant because 10 is inside the interval in this trial
The true effect is exactly 10 percent
correctAnswer: The interval includes zero, so the difference is not significant
explanation: An absolute risk reduction whose 95 percent confidence interval includes zero is not statistically significant. The point estimate of 10 percent is compatible with both benefit and harm. "The point estimate proves a clear 10 percent benefit" is not the best choice because a positive point estimate does not establish an effect when the interval crosses zero. "The negative bound proves the drug is harmful" is not the best choice because the interval also includes benefit, so harm is not proved. "The true effect is exactly 10 percent" is not the best choice because the interval is a range of compatible values, not a single exact effect. "The result is significant because 10 is inside the interval in this trial" is not the best choice because significance for this difference depends on whether zero is excluded, not on whether the point estimate sits inside its own interval.

references.label: Altman. Confidence intervals for the number needed to treat. A confidence interval for absolute risk reduction that includes zero is not a significant difference. PMC1114210.

blueprintTopic: Relative risk reduction can dwarf the absolute benefit
vignette: In a trial, the outcome occurs in 4 of 100 people on placebo and in 2 of 100 people on the new drug. A headline says the drug cuts risk in half. No one is lost to follow-up. You are asked how many people must be treated to prevent one event.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Number needed to treat is 2
Number needed to treat is 96
Number needed to treat is 4
Number needed to treat is 50
Number needed to treat cannot be calculated
correctAnswer: Number needed to treat is 50
explanation: The relative risk reduction is 50 percent, but the absolute risk reduction is 4 percent minus 2 percent, which is 2 percentage points. Number needed to treat is 1 divided by 0.02, which is 50. The headline describes the relative change, not the absolute one. "Number needed to treat is 2" is not the best choice because 2 is the absolute percentage-point difference, not the number needed to treat. "Number needed to treat is 4" is not the best choice because 4 percent is the placebo event rate. "Number needed to treat is 96" is not the best choice because 96 is neither the reciprocal of the absolute reduction nor the event count. "Number needed to treat cannot be calculated" is not the best choice because both event rates are known.

references.label: Irwig et al. Smart Health Choices. Distinguish relative risk reduction from absolute risk reduction. Number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction. NCBI Bookshelf NBK63647.

blueprintTopic: Intention-to-treat keeps the randomized groups
vignette: In a trial, 200 patients are randomized to surgery and 200 to medical therapy. Forty surgical patients never receive surgery and are analyzed by some authors with the medical group. You must choose the analysis that preserves randomization for the policy question of assigning surgery.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Move the forty into the medical group
Analyze everyone in the group originally assigned
Analyze patients if they received surgery for this patient
Analyze patients who felt better
Drop the forty patients from the trial
correctAnswer: Analyze everyone in the group originally assigned
explanation: Intention-to-treat analyzes participants in the groups to which they were randomized, whether or not they received the treatment. That comparison estimates the effect of the assignment. Moving untreated patients into the other group breaks randomization. "Analyze patients if they received surgery for this patient" is not the best choice because That is a per-protocol view and can be biased by why people skipped surgery. "Drop the forty patients from the trial" is not the best choice because Dropping them can unbalance the groups. "Move the forty into the medical group" is not the best choice because They were not randomized to medical therapy. "Analyze patients who felt better" is not the best choice because Outcome-based exclusion destroys the comparison.

references.label: Detry and Lewis. Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in the groups to which they were randomized. PMC5654877.

blueprintTopic: Diazepam for alcohol withdrawal when the liver is healthy
vignette: A 45-year-old man stops drinking 14 hours ago. He is tremulous, pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 156/96 mm Hg. CIWA-Ar score is 16. He has no jaundice, albumin is 4.2 g/dL, and INR is 1.0. He has had a prior withdrawal seizure. Glucose is 96 mg/dL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge with advice to taper beer
Haloperidol as the drug
Phenytoin loading and no benzodiazepine
Diazepam with symptom-triggered doses
Propranolol as monotherapy
correctAnswer: Diazepam with symptom-triggered doses
explanation: Alcohol withdrawal with a high CIWA-Ar score is treated with a benzodiazepine. When there is no important liver dysfunction, diazepam is a first-line choice because of rapid onset and a long duration. Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin are not the treatment of withdrawal seizures. "Phenytoin loading and no benzodiazepine" is not the best choice because Withdrawal seizures are treated with benzodiazepines, not phenytoin monotherapy. "Haloperidol as the drug" is not the best choice because An antipsychotic does not treat the withdrawal syndrome and can lower the seizure threshold. "Discharge with advice to taper beer" is not the best choice because He is in significant withdrawal with a seizure history. "Propranolol as monotherapy" is not the best choice because A beta blocker may blunt vital signs and hide worsening withdrawal.

references.label: StatPearls. Alcohol withdrawal. Diazepam is first-line when hepatic dysfunction is not a concern.

blueprintTopic: Lorazepam when withdrawal occurs with liver failure
vignette: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis stops drinking. He is tremulous and diaphoretic. Bilirubin is 4.8 mg/dL, albumin is 2.4 g/dL, and INR is 1.9. Pulse is 120/min and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. CIWA-Ar score is 18. Glucose is 88 mg/dL. He has asterixis.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Phenytoin as the sedative
Chlordiazepoxide because it is long-acting
A large loading dose of diazepam
Lorazepam rather than diazepam
Lactulose and no benzodiazepine
correctAnswer: Lorazepam rather than diazepam
explanation: Benzodiazepines still treat the withdrawal. Diazepam is avoided when hepatic dysfunction is significant because of its long-acting metabolites. Lorazepam is an alternative when diazepam is not a good option. "A large loading dose of diazepam" is not the best choice because Long-acting diazepam is the drug the guidance sets aside in liver failure. "Phenytoin as the sedative" is not the best choice because Phenytoin does not treat alcohol withdrawal. "Lactulose and no benzodiazepine" is not the best choice because He may also have encephalopathy, but untreated withdrawal is dangerous. Lactulose does not replace a benzodiazepine. "Chlordiazepoxide because it is long-acting" is not the best choice because Another long-acting benzodiazepine has the same problem in liver failure.

references.label: StatPearls. Alcohol withdrawal. If diazepam is not appropriate because of liver dysfunction, lorazepam can be used.

blueprintTopic: Stop the serotonergic drugs in serotonin syndrome
vignette: A 30-year-old woman started tramadol yesterday for back pain. She takes fluoxetine. She is agitated, febrile to 38.9 C, and has inducible clonus and hyperreflexia. Pulse is 122/min and blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg. Creatine kinase is 400 U/L. Pupils are dilated.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Dantrolene as the first drug
Give another dose of fluoxetine
Continue both drugs and add cyproheptadine for this patient
Start haloperidol for the agitation
Stop fluoxetine and tramadol and support her
correctAnswer: Stop fluoxetine and tramadol and support her
explanation: Clonus, hyperreflexia, fever, and agitation within a day of adding a serotonergic drug are serotonin syndrome. The first step is to stop the serotonergic drugs and support the patient. Adding more serotonin is harmful. "Give another dose of fluoxetine" is not the best choice because More serotonergic drug worsens the syndrome. "Start haloperidol for the agitation" is not the best choice because The diagnosis is toxicity, not a primary psychotic agitation to be treated by continuing the cause. "Continue both drugs and add cyproheptadine for this patient" is not the best choice because An antidote does not replace stopping the offending drugs.
