Cyproheptadine is not first while the drugs continue. "Dantrolene as the first drug" is not the best choice because Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and is not the first step here. The drug exposure must stop.

references.label: StatPearls. Serotonin syndrome. Discontinue serotonergic agents first and give supportive care.

blueprintTopic: Valve replacement for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis
vignette: A 76-year-old man has severe aortic stenosis with a mean gradient of 48 mm Hg and a valve area of 0.8 cm2. He has exertional syncope and dyspnea. Ejection fraction is 60 percent. Blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. He has no other active illness. He asks whether pills can replace a valve procedure.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Refer for aortic valve replacement
Start a beta blocker and recheck in two years
Anticoagulation as a substitute for a new valve
Balloon valvuloplasty as definitive treatment
Medical therapy and no valve procedure
correctAnswer: Refer for aortic valve replacement
explanation: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is treated with valve replacement, surgical or transcatheter. Medicines do not change the natural history. Balloon valvuloplasty is a short-lived bridge, not definitive care. "Medical therapy and no valve procedure" is not the best choice because Once symptoms start, survival is poor without replacement. "Balloon valvuloplasty as definitive treatment" is not the best choice because The benefit of balloon dilation is temporary. "Start a beta blocker and recheck in two years" is not the best choice because A two-year delay is not appropriate after syncope. "Anticoagulation as a substitute for a new valve" is not the best choice because Anticoagulation does not relieve fixed obstruction.

references.label: StatPearls. Aortic stenosis. Valve replacement is indicated for symptomatic severe stenosis. Medical therapy does not alter progression.

blueprintTopic: One-time ultrasound for abdominal aortic aneurysm
vignette: A 67-year-old man smoked a pack daily until age 60. He has no abdominal symptoms. Blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. He has never had an abdominal ultrasound. He asks which one-time screening test is recommended for him.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Mesenteric duplex as the screening test
Annual CT angiogram of the aorta
Coronary calcium scoring instead
No vascular screening at this age
One-time ultrasound for aortic aneurysm
correctAnswer: One-time ultrasound for aortic aneurysm
explanation: USPSTF recommends one-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men 65 to 75 years old who have ever smoked. He is in that group. Annual CT and unrelated vascular tests are not the recommendation. "Annual CT angiogram of the aorta" is not the best choice because Screening is a one-time ultrasound, not annual CT. "No vascular screening at this age" is not the best choice because He meets both the age band and the smoking criterion. "Mesenteric duplex as the screening test" is not the best choice because Mesenteric imaging is not the aneurysm screen. "Coronary calcium scoring instead" is not the best choice because Calcium scoring does not look for an abdominal aneurysm.

references.label: USPSTF. One-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men ages 65 to 75 who have ever smoked.

blueprintTopic: Add colchicine for acute pericarditis
vignette: A 29-year-old man has sharp chest pain that is worse supine and better sitting forward. A rub is present. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and PR depression. Troponin is normal. He has no ulcer disease and normal kidneys. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. You plan anti-inflammatory therapy.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Colchicine is avoided in a first episode
Ibuprofen plus colchicine
Prednisone as the first drug
Antibiotics for presumed bacterial pericarditis
Heparin and urgent catheterization
correctAnswer: Ibuprofen plus colchicine
explanation: Idiopathic acute pericarditis is treated with an NSAID plus colchicine. Colchicine shortens the attack and cuts recurrence roughly in half. Catheterization is for coronary occlusion, which this ECG pattern and normal troponin do not suggest. "Colchicine is avoided in a first episode" is not the best choice because Colchicine is used in the first episode to prevent recurrence. "Heparin and urgent catheterization" is not the best choice because Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression and a rub is pericarditis, not an occluded artery. "Prednisone as the first drug" is not the best choice because Steroids are not first-line and are associated with recurrence. "Antibiotics for presumed bacterial pericarditis" is not the best choice because He is not septic, and viral or idiopathic pericarditis is far more common.

references.label: StatPearls. Pericarditis. Colchicine added to anti-inflammatory therapy reduces recurrence.
